checkpoints.practiceTask: Inspect your current project directory and verify `uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000` boots cleanly inside a fresh `.venv` created strictly from `requirements.txt`.
acceptanceCriteria: Service runs inside a fresh virtual environment without extra manual `pip install` guesses.
Uses `--host 0.0.0.0` in container launch command rather than localhost-only loopback binding.
commonMistakes: Binding `--host 127.0.0.1` inside a container (Docker proxy / external traffic gets Connection Refused!).
Forgetting a library in `requirements.txt` that happened to exist globally on dev machine.
Using relative paths like `open('data.json')` that break when launched from another working directory.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why must `uvicorn app.main:app` use `--host 0.0.0.0` (instead of `127.0.0.1`) inside a deployed Docker container?

options.text: `127.0.0.1` only accepts traffic originating inside the same container; `0.0.0.0` lets Docker port forwarding and reverse proxies reach the app.
options.explanation: Correct! Binding only to loopback inside a container blocks incoming requests from outside that container.

options.text: Because `0.0.0.0` encrypts HTTP automatically into HTTPS.
options.explanation: TLS requires a proxy or certificate; `0.0.0.0` controls listening network interfaces.

options.text: Because `127.0.0.1` disables Pydantic validation.
options.explanation: Host binding governs socket network listening, not Pydantic.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Bind container servers to `0.0.0.0` so reverse proxies and container networks can reach them.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why pin dependency versions (e.g. lockfile or `requirements.txt` with `==`) before shipping?

options.text: So production containers install the exact tested package versions instead of silently pulling breaking upstream updates weeks later.
options.explanation: Correct! Reproducible builds prevent surprise crashes from unpinned upgrades.

options.text: To make Docker images larger.
options.explanation: Version pinning guarantees stability, not image bloat.

options.text: To bypass Python virtual environments.
options.explanation: Lockfiles complement virtualenvs and containers.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Pin package versions and validate clean installation from scratch.

checkpoints.title: Dockerfiles and Containers
checkpoints.summary: Build lean, non-root production Docker images for FastAPI and Compose multi-service stacks alongside n8n.
learningObjectives: Write a clean production `Dockerfile` using slim base images, `.dockerignore`, layer caching, and a non-root user.
Never bake `.env` or secret files into `COPY . .` image layers.
Verify multi-container DNS (`http://triage-api:8000`) inside `compose.yaml`.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Think of a **Docker image** like a sealed shipping crate containing exact Python, system libraries, and your code—so whether it runs on your laptop, a \$6 VPS, or a cloud platform, it behaves identically! A **Dockerfile** is the recipe that builds that crate. Watch out for two classic traps: (1) forgetting `.dockerignore`, which accidentally copies your `.venv` AND `.env` secrets right into the image layer, and (2) running containers as `root` unnecessarily.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Dockerfile optimization & hygiene: use `python:3.12-slim`; `COPY requirements.txt .` BEFORE `COPY app/ ./app` so Docker caches pip installs cleanly across code edits; exclude `.venv`, `.git`, `.env`, `__pycache__` via `.dockerignore`; create a non-root OS user (`useradd --create-home appuser` + `USER appuser`); set `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1` and `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` so structured JSON logs stream immediately without buffering.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Clean Dockerfiles eliminate OS drift, protect image security via non-root users, and make `docker compose up` reliable across environments.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Whenever deploying FastAPI, background workers, vector DBs, or n8n reproducibly onto VPS or container platforms.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't put `ARG OPENAI_API_KEY=...` or `COPY .env` inside a Dockerfile—secrets baked into image layers stay readable via `docker history`!

examples.title: Production Slim FastAPI Dockerfile + .dockerignore
examples.description: Caches dependencies, drops root privileges, and streams JSON logs immediately.
examples.code:
# .dockerignore (CRITICAL!)
# .venv/
# .env
# .git/
# __pycache__/

# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

RUN useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash appuser
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser app ./app
USER appuser

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

checkpoints.practiceTask: Spot the order mistake if you put `COPY . .` BEFORE `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`, and verify why `.dockerignore` must include `.env` and `.venv`.
acceptanceCriteria: Explains why changing one line in `app/main.py` invalidates slow `pip install` layer caching if `COPY . .` comes first.
Verifies `.env` never gets baked into image layers and container runs as non-root `appuser`.
commonMistakes: Missing `.dockerignore` -> copying `.env` secrets and gigabytes of `.venv` into the Docker build context!
Running containers as `root` with write privileges across host mounts.
Omitting `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` so print/JSON logs sit invisible in memory until crash.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why MUST `.env` be listed inside `.dockerignore` before running `COPY . .` in a `Dockerfile`?

options.text: Without `.dockerignore`, `COPY . .` bakes local `.env` secrets directly into the container image layers—exposing them to anyone with image access.
options.explanation: Correct! Inject runtime secrets via `-e` or Compose `env_file` at container start, never inside built image layers.

options.text: Because Docker refuses to boot if an image contains hidden files.
options.explanation: Docker silently copies `.env` into image layers unless ignored—which is why it's dangerous.

options.text: Because `.dockerignore` installs Python dependencies automatically.
options.explanation: `.dockerignore` filters the build context files.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Exclude `.env`, `.venv`, and `.git` via `.dockerignore`; inject runtime secrets only at container run time.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why put `COPY requirements.txt .` + `RUN pip install` BEFORE `COPY app ./app` in a Dockerfile?

options.text: Docker caches unchanged earlier layers, so editing Python app code rebuilds in seconds without reinstalling packages every time.
options.explanation: Correct! Proper layer ordering speeds up builds dramatically.

options.text: Because `pip install` deletes the `app/` directory otherwise.
options.explanation: Unrelated—layer cache reuse is the reason.

options.text: Because non-root users cannot read `requirements.txt`.
options.explanation: Layer caching efficiency is why dependencies go first.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Order Dockerfile steps from least-frequently changed (dependencies) to most-frequently changed (app source).

checkpoints.title: Environment Configuration and Secret Management
checkpoints.summary: Validate required environment settings on boot with Pydantic `BaseSettings`, separate dev/prod configs, and never hardcode keys.
learningObjectives: Fail fast on startup if a required API key, webhook secret, or database URL is missing or malformed.
Inject secrets cleanly at runtime via environment variables / secret stores (Docker Compose `env_file`, platform Secrets UI).
Provide `.env.example` with safe placeholder keys so contributors know required variables.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Imagine deploying a container on Friday night, seeing HTTP 200 on startup, and discovering Monday morning every triage call crashed because `SERVICE_BEARER_TOKEN` was misspelled! Using Pydantic `BaseSettings`, your FastAPI app checks every required env variable at **boot time** and refuses to start silently misconfigured. Meanwhile, secrets live strictly outside code—injected at runtime by your host/VPS/PaaS, never baked into Git or Docker images.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Separate **Configuration** (non-sensitive behavior toggles like `LOG_LEVEL`, `MODEL_NAME`, `REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SEC`, `ENV=prod`) from **Secrets** (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `WEBHOOK_HMAC_SECRET`, `DB_PASSWORD`). Use `pydantic-settings` (`BaseSettings`) with strict non-empty validation on secrets so missing vars raise crisp `ValidationError` on import/startup instead of crashing mid-request hours later. Never log `settings.model_dump()` without redacting `SecretStr` fields.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Fail-fast config validation prevents mysterious partial outages, while runtime-only secret injection keeps keys safe across Git and Docker registries.
checkpoints.whenToUse: In every deployed FastAPI app, background worker, and Compose stack.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never assign production secret values as default strings in Python (`api_key: str = 'sk-real-default'`)!

examples.title: Fail-Fast Config Validation Using SecretStr
examples.description: Refuses startup immediately if required runtime secrets are missing or blank.
examples.code:
from pydantic import Field, SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    environment: str = "production"
    model_name: str = "gpt-4o-mini"
    request_timeout_sec: float = Field(default=10.0, gt=0, le=60)
    internal_bearer_token: SecretStr  # Required: zero default!
    webhook_hmac_secret: SecretStr    # Required: zero default!
    llm_api_key: SecretStr            # Required: zero default!

# Calling Settings() at boot validates env vars cleanly and avoids printing secrets in repr()!

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write a `.env.example` template matching the `Settings` class above with clear comments indicating format and zero real credentials.
acceptanceCriteria: Uses safe dummy placeholders (`CHANGE_ME`) instead of real credentials.
Marks secret variables as `SecretStr` without insecure fallback defaults.
commonMistakes: Logging `print(settings)` accidentally when secrets are stored as plain strings instead of `SecretStr`.
Providing weak fallback defaults like `secret: str = 'dev-secret-123'` in production config!
Checking `os.getenv('API_KEY')` deep inside helper functions instead of validating everything once at startup.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why are `SecretStr` fields with NO default value superior to `os.getenv('WEBHOOK_SECRET', 'default-123')` in production config?

options.text: Missing secrets fail loudly at boot instead of silently accepting an insecure guessable `'default-123'` signature in production.
options.explanation: Correct! Fail-closed startup validation prevents accidental insecure deployments.

options.text: Because `os.getenv` cannot read string variables.
options.explanation: `os.getenv` reads strings fine—weak defaults are the dangerous flaw.

options.text: Because `SecretStr` deletes `.env` files after reading.
options.explanation: `SecretStr` prevents accidental string printing/logging.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Validate all required config at startup and never give secrets weak fallback defaults.

quizQuestions.prompt: Where should runtime secrets (`LLM_API_KEY`, `WEBHOOK_HMAC_SECRET`) be supplied when running Docker in production?

options.text: Injected at container runtime via host platform secrets UI / restricted `.env` file mounted via `env_file`—never inside Dockerfile or Git.
options.explanation: Correct! Runtime injection keeps secrets out of version control and container image registries.

options.text: Committed to a private GitHub branch named `secrets`.
options.explanation: Git history preserves secrets permanently and exposes them across clones.

options.text: Hardcoded directly inside `schemas.py`.
options.explanation: Never hardcode secrets in code.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Keep secrets completely out of Git and Docker image builds; inject at runtime.

checkpoints.title: Where Services Actually Run
checkpoints.summary: Build an accurate mental map of processes, compute hosts, networks, and edges—eliminating confusion between your code host and Cloudflare/DNS.
learningObjectives: Trace physically which CPU/RAM machine executes your n8n container, FastAPI container, and vector database.
Distinguish where computation runs (origin host) from DNS/CDN/tunnel layers in front of it.
Diagnose why closing your laptop stops services hosted locally—even behind a public domain or tunnel.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Here is a confusion that trips up almost everyone moving from n8n tutorials to deployment: *'I set up a domain and Cloudflare Tunnel—so my API is in the cloud now, right?'* **NO!** Ask one grounding question every time: **Which physical computer's CPU and RAM is actually running `uvicorn` and `n8n` right now?** If it's your bedroom laptop, closing the lid puts the server to sleep and users get `502 Bad Gateway`! Cloudflare Tunnel only builds a protected road to your house; **hosting** provides the always-on power plant (VPS, cloud container, managed host) where your code lives 24/7.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Every production automation stack has distinct physical planes: (1) **Origin Compute Plane** (Linux VPS, Render/Railway/Fly/ECS container host) running n8n, FastAPI, Postgres/Qdrant containers; (2) **Network/Edge Plane** (DNS records, reverse proxy / Cloudflare Edge / Tunnel) forwarding HTTPS requests safely to origin sockets; (3) **External SaaS Plane** (LLM providers, Gmail, Slack). Tunnels connect Edge -> Origin cleanly across NAT/firewalls without providing CPU, memory, or persistent disk.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Knowing exact process residence immediately dissolves mystery errors like 'tunnel configured but 502 error' or 'why did cron stop when my laptop slept?'
checkpoints.whenToUse: Whenever designing deployment topology, quoting server uptime expectations, or debugging 502/530 connectivity issues.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never confuse domain registration (Namecheap/Cloudflare Registrar), DNS routing, or Cloudflare Tunnel with origin compute hosting.

examples.title: Physical Placement Map: Laptop Dev vs. Production VPS
examples.description: Always know which machine owns CPU/RAM vs which layer merely routes packets.
examples.code:
LOCAL DEV (Laptop runs origin):
  Internet Webhook -> Cloudflare Edge -> cloudflared -> Laptop Docker (stops if lid closes!)

PRODUCTION VPS / PAAS (Cloud host runs origin 24/7):
  Internet Webhook -> DNS / Reverse Proxy (TLS) -> Always-On VPS Docker Network:
      ├── caddy/nginx OR cloudflared
      ├── n8n (:5678)
      ├── fastapi-triage (:8000)
      └── postgres (:5432, internal Docker network only)

checkpoints.practiceTask: Draw the exact host diagram for your capstone project, labeling which single box actually executes Python, stores Postgres rows, and handles 24/7 webhooks.
acceptanceCriteria: Explicitly separates Edge/DNS/Tunnel from the Origin Compute machine executing containers.
Confirms databases stay private inside internal networks without public IP port exposure.
commonMistakes: Thinking buying a `.com` domain or adding Cloudflare DNS provides server hosting.
Deploying a production client webhook pointed at a tunnel running on your personal laptop.
Exposing Postgres `:5432` or Qdrant `:6333` on `0.0.0.0:5432` public host firewall.

quizQuestions.prompt: A learner runs FastAPI on their home laptop, points `api.myproject.com` via Cloudflare Tunnel to it, then turns off the laptop and travels. What happens when n8n sends a webhook?

options.text: Cloudflare returns an origin unreachable error (`502`/`530`) because Cloudflare Tunnel routes traffic—it does NOT host or execute your Python code.
options.explanation: Correct! Always host continuous production backends on always-on VPS or cloud container compute.

options.text: Cloudflare automatically copies and runs Python containers on Cloudflare edge nodes.
options.explanation: Cloudflare Tunnel forwards connections to your running origin; it does not run Docker Python apps.

options.text: Wait 5 minutes and DNS runs FastAPI for free.
options.explanation: DNS translates hostnames to IPs/tunnels—it never executes app code.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Ask 'Which machine owns CPU/RAM for this process?'—tunnels route traffic, hosts run code.

quizQuestions.prompt: Should your Postgres or Redis database port (`5432`/`6379`) be exposed to the public internet alongside FastAPI?

options.text: No—keep databases bound inside private Docker/VPC networks accessible only by your backend services.
options.explanation: Correct! Expose only TLS-terminated HTTP/proxy ingress publicly; lock databases inside private networks.

options.text: Yes, so external scanners can verify it's running.
options.explanation: Exposed database ports invite brute-force attacks and immediate compromise.

options.text: Yes, otherwise n8n webhooks can't trigger FastAPI.
options.explanation: n8n talks to FastAPI over HTTP, not directly to internal ports unless intentionally integrated privately.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Keep databases private behind internal container/VPC networks.

checkpoints.title: Choosing Hosting Options Pragmatically
checkpoints.summary: Match hosting tiers—managed PaaS, single VPS with Compose, or serverless/workers—to team size, stateful needs, and operational skill.
learningObjectives: Compare Managed PaaS (Railway/Fly/Render/Cloud Run), Single Linux VPS + Docker Compose, and Edge Workers/Serverless.
Understand why long-running background queues and local Docker Compose bundles fit VPS/containers better than tiny short-timeout serverless limits.
Pick the simplest maintainable host that supports reliable backups, TLS, and env secrets.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Don't spin up complex 12-node Kubernetes clusters for a single FastAPI service and n8n! Choose the simplest reliable home that fits how your code runs: (1) **Managed PaaS** (push Git/Dockerfile -> HTTPS URL automatically, great when you don't want Linux OS patching); (2) **Single Linux VPS + Docker Compose** (one \$6–\$20 server running n8n + FastAPI + Postgres + Caddy/Tunnel cleanly in one `compose.yaml`—predictable cost, full Docker freedom); (3) **Serverless / Edge Functions** (instant scale for short stateless HTTP glue, awkward if you need persistent Python RAG libraries or 2-minute tasks).
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Evaluate hosting by operational constraints: (a) **Execution duration & cold starts** (LangGraph/LLM calls take seconds—cold-boot serverless or 10s edge limits bite fast); (b) **Stateful storage** (n8n SQLite/Postgres + LangGraph checkpointers + local volumes require persistent disks, NOT ephemeral stateless containers!); (c) **Ops burden** (VPS requires firewalling `ufw`, unattended OS upgrades, and disk backups; managed PaaS charges extra to handle TLS/rollouts for you).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Picking right-sized hosting avoids drowning solo projects in Kubernetes YAML OR getting locked out by ephemeral disks wiping n8n/checkpointer state.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before provisioning production accounts; match stateful needs and ops skills intentionally.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never deploy stateful n8n SQLite files or local vector indexes onto ephemeral containers with zero persistent volume!

examples.title: Hosting Trade-Off Matrix for Automation Stacks
examples.description: Select infrastructure matching persistence needs and maintenance budget.
examples.code:
1. Managed PaaS (Render / Railway / Cloud Run + Managed Postgres):
   + Fast Git push deploys, automatic HTTPS, zero Linux patching
   - Higher per-service cost; watch ephemeral disk traps (use managed DB!)

2. Single VPS + Docker Compose + Caddy / Cloudflare Tunnel:
   + Fixed monthly cost, co-locates n8n + FastAPI + Postgres + Redis cleanly
   - You own OS security updates, firewall (`ufw`), and volume backups!

3. Edge / Serverless (Cloudflare Workers / Lambda):
   + Zero idle server maintenance; ideal for lightweight webhook signing or proxies
   - Tight CPU/memory/duration caps; poor fit for stateful n8n or heavy Python libs

checkpoints.practiceTask: Choose between Managed PaaS and Single VPS + Compose for your own capstone project and list 2 maintenance responsibilities you accept with that choice.
acceptanceCriteria: Identifies persistent database/volume requirement explicitly (never ephemeral disk loss!).
Lists realistic ops ownership (backups, OS/TLS renewals or cost alerts).
commonMistakes: Hosting n8n or Postgres inside an ephemeral cloud container without persistent volume/DB—wiping all workflows on redeploy!
Deploying Kubernetes prematurely for a 2-container solo portfolio app.
Leaving default VPS SSH password authentication open to the internet instead of SSH keys + firewall.

quizQuestions.prompt: You deploy n8n (default SQLite mode) to a container platform without attaching a persistent volume or external Postgres database, then redeploy a config tweak. What happens?

options.text: Ephemeral container storage resets on redeploy—wiping your saved workflows, credentials, and execution history!
options.explanation: Correct! Stateful tools like n8n and LangGraph checkpointers MUST persist to a managed database or persistent disk.

options.text: Docker automatically backs up SQLite inside Git.
options.explanation: Container filesystems never write back to Git.

options.text: HTTP automatically migrates state to Cloudflare Workers.
options.explanation: State requires explicit persistent storage.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Always connect stateful apps (n8n, checkpointers, vector stores) to durable databases or backed-up persistent volumes.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which workload fits Cloudflare Workers / lightweight edge functions BEST without wrestling infrastructure?

options.text: Tiny ultra-fast stateless tasks like verifying incoming webhook HMAC headers or routing requests near users.
options.explanation: Correct! Short stateless HTTP edge logic plays to Workers' strengths; heavy stateful Python/n8n stacks fit VPS/containers.

options.text: Hosting a full Docker Compose stack containing n8n, Postgres, and local embedding models.
options.explanation: Containers with stateful DBs belong on VPS/PaaS compute, not edge JS isolates.

options.text: Replacing Postgres long-term relational storage.
options.explanation: Use real databases for relational state.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Use edge functions for fast stateless routing/verification; use containers/VPS + managed DBs for stateful Python & n8n.

checkpoints.title: Domains and DNS Records in Production
checkpoints.summary: Wire subdomains (`n8n.domain.com`, `api.domain.com`) with `A`/`AAAA`/`CNAME` records cleanly and diagnose DNS propagation issues.
learningObjectives: Separate services cleanly onto dedicated subdomains (`n8n.example.com`, `api.example.com`).
Understand `A` (IPv4), `AAAA` (IPv6), `CNAME` (alias to hostname/tunnel), and `TTL` propagation.
Diagnose `NXDOMAIN` or stale DNS responses using `dig` / `nslookup`.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Giving n8n and FastAPI separate clean subdomains—like `flow.acme-ops.com` and `api.acme-ops.com`—keeps webhooks, TLS certificates, and access rules clean and flexible. Inside your DNS control panel (e.g., Cloudflare DNS), an **`A` record** points a name to an IPv4 server address (`203.0.113.10`), while a **`CNAME` record** points one hostname to another hostname (like a managed PaaS target or Cloudflare Tunnel UUID hostname). Lowering `TTL` before migrations prevents waiting hours for old cached DNS records to expire!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: DNS record patterns: `A` maps hostname -> IPv4; `AAAA` -> IPv6; `CNAME` -> canonical target hostname (cannot sit directly on apex `@` without provider CNAME flattening). When DNS is **proxied** (Cloudflare orange cloud), public `dig api.example.com` returns Cloudflare Edge IPs rather than your raw origin IP, masking origin DDoS targets while terminating TLS at edge. Always lower TTL (e.g., `60–300s`) 24 hours prior to server cutovers.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Understanding DNS prevents terrifying 'I switched servers why are half our webhooks hitting the old server?' outages.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Whenever provisioning public webhook domains, staging environments, or migrating backend servers.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't point webhooks directly at ephemeral raw dynamic home IPs—use static IPs, dynamic DNS/tunnels, or managed PaaS CNAMEs.

examples.title: Clean Subdomain DNS Layout & Quick Diagnostic Command
examples.description: Separate n8n ingress, FastAPI service, and verify resolution live via `dig`.
examples.code:
# Example DNS table:
# A     n8n.acme-ops.com     -> 203.0.113.42        (VPS IP, Proxied)
# CNAME api.acme-ops.com     -> <tunnel-id>.cfargotunnel.com (Proxied)

# Verify DNS resolution from terminal:
dig +short api.acme-ops.com
# If returns empty -> NXDOMAIN / typo or record missing!
# Check HTTPS + TLS handshake after DNS resolves:
curl -Iv https://api.acme-ops.com/health

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write a DNS table giving separate subdomains to an n8n server on a static IP VPS and a FastAPI app routed via a managed PaaS CNAME, plus test one command verifying resolution.
acceptanceCriteria: Uses `A` record for raw IPv4 VPS and `CNAME` for hostname target.
Explains TTL impact during migrations and verifies via `dig`/`curl -Iv`.
commonMistakes: Putting a literal `http://` or port `:8000` inside a DNS `A` or `CNAME` record (DNS only maps hostnames—ports & schemes belong in URLs/proxies!).
Keeping 24-hour TTL right before switching production server IPs.
Putting n8n and FastAPI on sloppy conflicting URL paths before understanding reverse proxies.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can't you enter `203.0.113.42:8000` inside a DNS `A` record?

options.text: DNS only maps hostnames to IP addresses (ports and HTTP paths belong in your reverse proxy / URL, or SRV records for specific services).
options.explanation: Correct! Point DNS at the IP (`203.0.113.42`), then let Caddy/Nginx/Cloudflare route port 443 HTTPS internally to `:8000`.

options.text: Because DNS prohibits port 8000 globally.
options.explanation: DNS simply translates names to network addresses; ports live at TCP transport + proxy config.

options.text: Because only IPv6 allows ports in DNS.
options.explanation: Neither A nor AAAA carries port numbers.

quizQuestions.takeaway: DNS maps domain -> IP/target hostname; reverse proxies map standard HTTPS (:443) -> app ports (:8000/:5678).

quizQuestions.prompt: You run `curl https://api.example.com/health` and get `Could not resolve host: api.example.com`. What layer failed?

options.text: DNS lookup failed (`NXDOMAIN`/missing record or local resolver issue)—traffic never even reached FastAPI.
options.explanation: Correct! Fix the DNS record or hostname spelling before debugging FastAPI code.

options.text: Pydantic threw a 422 error.
options.explanation: HTTP never connected if DNS could not resolve the host.

options.text: CORS headers are missing.
options.explanation: CORS runs in browsers after HTTP connects.

quizQuestions.takeaway: `Could not resolve host` is always DNS/hostname configuration—never app logic.

checkpoints.title: Reverse Proxies and TLS Termination
checkpoints.summary: Place Caddy or Nginx in front of FastAPI and n8n to terminate HTTPS cleanly, forward headers accurately, and enforce size/rate limits.
learningObjectives: Configure a clean reverse proxy (`Caddy` / `Nginx`) listening on `443 HTTPS` and forwarding internally to `:8000` / `:5678`.
Preserve `Host`, `X-Forwarded-For`, and `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers so backend apps know the true external HTTPS scheme.
Verify end-to-end TLS termination vs HTTP plaintext inside private container links.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Why shouldn't Python `uvicorn` directly manage SSL certificates on port 443 in production? Because a lightweight **reverse proxy** like **Caddy** or **Nginx** handles automatic Let's Encrypt HTTPS certificates, HTTP->HTTPS redirects, request size limits, timeouts, and routing `flow.example.com` -> `n8n:5678` + `api.example.com` -> `fastapi:8000` all from one clean file! Inside the private Docker network, the proxy speaks fast HTTP directly to your containers, while **outside** on the internet, 100% of traffic travels encrypted via TLS!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Reverse proxy duties: (1) Terminate external TLS 1.2/1.3 (`https://` on `:443`) using automated ACME/Let's Encrypt certs or Cloudflare Origin Certificates; (2) Forward accurate proxy metadata (`X-Forwarded-Proto: https`, `X-Forwarded-For`, `Host`) so frameworks generate accurate callback/webhook URLs; (3) Configure appropriate proxy timeouts (`proxy_read_timeout` if synchronous requests exceed default 60s) and `client_max_body_size` guards.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Reverse proxies centralize HTTPS certificates, protect internal app ports, and prevent subtle `http://` redirect bugs when apps sit behind TLS termination.
checkpoints.whenToUse: On every VPS or container host exposing HTTP services to browsers, webhooks, or external APIs.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't expose raw Uvicorn/HTTP ports `:8000` directly on public firewall interfaces alongside your proxy—block `:8000` externally so all traffic must traverse HTTPS + proxy rules!

examples.title: Automatic HTTPS Reverse Proxy Config (Caddyfile)
examples.description: Routes clean subdomains to internal Compose services with automatic TLS certificates.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write the `Caddyfile` (or Nginx block) routing two subdomains (`n8n.mydomain.com` and `api.mydomain.com`) to Compose services while capping FastAPI request body sizes at `2MB`.
acceptanceCriteria: Terminates TLS cleanly on port 443 and proxies to internal Docker service names.
Includes protective request size limits and leaves internal service ports unexposed to public firewall.
commonMistakes: Exposing BOTH port `443` (Nginx/Caddy) AND port `8000` publicly on the VPS firewall—letting attackers bypass proxy security directly via `:8000`!
Dropping `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers so apps redirect clients from `https://` down to broken `http://` links.
Forgetting Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode ('Full (Strict)' vs broken 'Flexible' redirect loops!).

quizQuestions.prompt: You set up Caddy/Nginx with HTTPS on port 443 forwarding to FastAPI on port 8000, but forgot to close firewall port 8000 on your VPS. What risk exists?

options.text: Anyone can hit `http://your-vps-ip:8000` in plaintext bypassing HTTPS, Cloudflare edge, rate limits, and proxy rules.
options.explanation: Correct! Only expose 80/443 (or outbound tunnel); bind/firewall app ports internally.

options.text: FastAPI automatically disables Pydantic if port 8000 is open.
options.explanation: Pydantic still runs, but your proxy protections and TLS enforcement are bypassed.

options.text: Caddy refuses to forward traffic unless port 8000 is world-writable.
options.explanation: Caddy connects over loopback or the private Docker network without needing public exposure.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Terminate TLS at your reverse proxy and keep app ports closed to the public firewall.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does Cloudflare SSL mode `'Flexible'` often cause infinite `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` when paired with an origin reverse proxy enforcing HTTPS?

options.text: Flexible sends plain HTTP to your origin proxy, your origin responds with a 301 redirect back to HTTPS, looping infinitely—use `Full (Strict)` with valid origin certs instead.
options.explanation: Correct! Always use end-to-end TLS (`Full (Strict)`) with a valid Let's Encrypt or Cloudflare Origin Certificate.

options.text: Because Flexible disables DNS resolution.
options.explanation: DNS still resolves; protocol mismatch causes redirect loops.

options.text: Because HTTP POST converts into GET automatically.
options.explanation: Protocol redirect mismatches drive the loop.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Use `Full (Strict)` TLS mode with real origin certs or Cloudflare Tunnel—never plaintext `Flexible`.

checkpoints.title: Exposing n8n and Python APIs Safely
checkpoints.summary: Apply layered defenses—authentication, webhook signature checks, firewall minimization, and proxy rate limits—before exposing automation endpoints.
learningObjectives: Harden public endpoints with HTTPS + cryptographic auth (HMAC webhook signatures, bearer tokens, basic/OIDC SSO for n8n UI).
Minimize public attack surface—keep internal-only endpoints unexposed unless genuinely needed by outside callers.
Verify every protected route returns `401`/`403` when tested unauthenticated from outside.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Here is a golden rule: **just because a URL isn't linked on Google doesn't mean bots won't hit it within 5 minutes!** Automated scanners hit every new public domain and IP continuously probing `/admin`, `/webhook`, `/v1/triage`, and `/openapi.json`. Before exposing n8n or FastAPI publicly: (1) Does FastAPI even *need* a public URL if only local Docker n8n calls it? If not, keep FastAPI strictly internal (`http://fastapi-triage:8000`)! (2) Every public endpoint MUST authenticate requests cryptographically (`Authorization: Bearer`, HMAC signature, or SSO), rate-limit bursts, and validate inputs strictly.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Attack surface reduction checklist: Keep internal microservices (`fastapi-triage`, `qdrant`, `postgres`) off public DNS entirely whenever only n8n talks to them! When public webhooks ARE required (e.g. Stripe -> n8n or remote callback -> FastAPI): enforce HTTPS + constant-time token/HMAC verification (`hmac.compare_digest`), validate strict Pydantic bounds (`max_length`), disable or protect `/docs`/`/openapi.json` if internal-only (`docs_url=None` in prod), and add reverse-proxy/Cloudflare WAF rate limiting.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Most production breaches in indie/SMB automations happen because a webhook or internal API endpoint was left public with zero authentication.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before deploying any workflow trigger or API endpoint reachable from the public internet.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't expose FastAPI publicly on internet DNS if n8n runs in the exact same Docker Compose network and is its ONLY caller!

examples.title: Internal-Only FastAPI vs. Public Authenticated Ingress
examples.description: Only expose what external callers genuinely need—keep internal microservices private.
examples.code:
# compose.yaml: ONLY reverse-proxy / n8n webhook URLs face public DNS!
services:
  n8n:
    image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n
    networks: [internal_net]
    # Reached via reverse proxy/Tunnel for UI & external SaaS webhooks ONLY

  fastapi-triage:
    build: ./triage_service
    networks: [internal_net]
    # Notice ZERO `ports:` exposed to host!
    # Reached cleanly by n8n via http://fastapi-triage:8000 + Bearer token.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Audit a 4-container stack (`proxy`, `n8n`, `fastapi-triage`, `postgres`): identify which service ports need public internet ingress, which need internal network only, and what auth protects each.
acceptanceCriteria: Blocks public ports on Postgres and internal-only FastAPI services.
Protects n8n UI + public webhooks with strong passwords/SSO + signed webhook secrets.
commonMistakes: Publishing `ports: - '8000:8000'` and `ports: - '5432:5432'` on a VPS where Docker bypasses `ufw` iptables by default!
Leaving n8n webhooks unauthenticated (`Authentication: None`) while trusting arbitrary incoming JSON payloads.
Forgetting that `SECURITY THROUGH OBSCURITY` (long random webhook UUID path alone) fails if URLs ever appear in browser history or logs.

quizQuestions.prompt: Your n8n instance and FastAPI service both run inside the same Docker Compose stack, and ONLY n8n calls FastAPI. What is the safest network architecture?

options.text: Keep FastAPI off public DNS and host ports (`expose` only on the private Compose network) while STILL enforcing a service bearer token.
options.explanation: Correct! Minimizing public exposure + keeping internal auth gives strong defense in depth.

options.text: Expose FastAPI on a public domain with zero auth since nobody knows the URL.
options.explanation: Obscurity isn't security; public scanners probe new subdomains immediately.

options.text: Publish FastAPI on port 80 without TLS.
options.explanation: Needless public exposure without encryption.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Don't expose internal-only backends publicly if Docker private networking already connects your caller.

quizQuestions.prompt: What subtle Docker + Linux firewall (`ufw`) surprise exposes containers accidentally to the world?

options.text: Binding `ports: ['8000:8000']` binds to `0.0.0.0` and writes Docker iptables rules that often bypass basic `ufw deny 8000` checks—bind `127.0.0.1:8000:8000` or omit `ports:` entirely.
options.explanation: Correct! Omitting unnecessary `ports:` or binding explicitly to `127.0.0.1` prevents accidental public exposure.

options.text: Docker refuses to build `Dockerfile` unless port 8000 is public.
options.explanation: Not true.

options.text: Python deletes `uvicorn` if UFW is installed.
options.explanation: Not true.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Omit host `ports:` or bind explicitly to `127.0.0.1:` when containers talk internally or via reverse proxy.

checkpoints.title: Webhook URL and Reverse Proxy Troubleshooting
checkpoints.summary: Fix classic behind-proxy bugs in n8n and FastAPI (`WEBHOOK_URL`, `N8N_PROXY_HOPS`, Slack signature mismatches, and `http://localhost:5678` links).
learningObjectives: Configure `WEBHOOK_URL` and `N8N_PROXY_HOPS` cleanly when running n8n behind Nginx, Caddy, or Cloudflare Tunnel.
Diagnose why n8n OAuth redirects or Webhook node URLs show `http://localhost:5678` instead of your HTTPS domain.
Verify forwarded headers (`X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Host`) when webhook HMAC signatures or URL generation fail.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Here is a classic post-deployment headache: you put n8n cleanly behind HTTPS `https://flow.company.com`, open the Webhook node UI, and it STILL displays `http://localhost:5678/webhook/...`, AND Google OAuth fails with `redirect_uri_mismatch`! Why? Because Caddy stripped TLS at the edge and spoke plain HTTP to n8n on port 5678—so n8n had no clue what public URL users actually see! Setting **`WEBHOOK_URL=https://flow.company.com/`** and **`N8N_PROXY_HOPS=1`** (plus forwarded proxy headers) tells n8n its true public identity immediately.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Critical reverse-proxy runtime variables for self-hosted n8n: `N8N_HOST=flow.company.com`, `N8N_PROTOCOL=https`, `WEBHOOK_URL=https://flow.company.com/`, `N8N_PROXY_HOPS=1` (matching proxy layer count for accurate IP rate limiting and cookies). In FastAPI behind a reverse proxy, start Uvicorn with `--proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips='*'` (restricted cleanly to proxy IP/CIDR when possible) so `request.url` reflects HTTPS correctly.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Fixing proxy env variables resolves OAuth callback failures, broken generated webhook URLs, and reverse-proxy IP spoofing in 2 minutes.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Whenever deploying self-hosted n8n or FastAPI behind Caddy, Nginx, Traefik, or Cloudflare Tunnel.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't skip checking proxy layers—if BOTH Cloudflare AND Caddy sit in front of n8n, set `N8N_PROXY_HOPS=2` accordingly and trust only local proxy subnets.

examples.title: Self-Hosted n8n Behind Reverse Proxy / Cloudflare Tunnel Env Vars
examples.description: Ensures generated webhook URLs, OAuth redirects, and client IP extraction work accurately.
examples.code:
# Essential n8n environment configuration behind HTTPS reverse proxy:
N8N_HOST=flow.acme-ops.com
N8N_PORT=5678
N8N_PROTOCOL=https
WEBHOOK_URL=https://flow.acme-ops.com/
N8N_PROXY_HOPS=1
# Note: Use N8N_PROXY_HOPS=2 if traffic traverses Cloudflare Edge -> Caddy -> n8n

# And in FastAPI container CMD when proxy headers matter:
# uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --proxy-headers

checkpoints.practiceTask: Diagnose why Google OAuth inside self-hosted n8n reports `Error 400: redirect_uri=http://localhost:5678/rest/oauth2-credential/callback` and write the exact env fix.
acceptanceCriteria: Sets `WEBHOOK_URL=https://<domain>/` and `N8N_PROTOCOL=https`.
Verifies `N8N_PROXY_HOPS` aligns with upstream reverse proxies.
commonMistakes: Leaving `WEBHOOK_URL` unset so n8n advertises `http://localhost:5678` in Webhook UI and OAuth callbacks.
Forgetting `N8N_PROXY_HOPS` behind reverse proxies, triggering express-rate-limit validation errors or wrong client IPs.
Omitting trailing slash or wrong scheme (`http://` vs `https://`) in `WEBHOOK_URL`.

quizQuestions.prompt: Self-hosted n8n runs behind HTTPS Caddy at `https://flow.acme.com`, yet OAuth login fails complaining `redirect_uri_mismatch` pointing to `http://localhost:5678/...`. Which setting fixes this?

options.text: Set `WEBHOOK_URL=https://flow.acme.com/` (plus `N8N_HOST`, `N8N_PROTOCOL=https`, `N8N_PROXY_HOPS`) and restart n8n.
options.explanation: Correct! `WEBHOOK_URL` configures the public externally reachable scheme and domain n8n advertises.

options.text: Change FastAPI CORS headers to `*`.
options.explanation: OAuth redirect URI mismatch is an n8n reverse-proxy URL config issue.

options.text: Reinstall Python `venv` inside n8n.
options.explanation: n8n is Node-based and needs `WEBHOOK_URL` set properly.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Configure `WEBHOOK_URL` and `N8N_PROXY_HOPS` whenever hosting n8n behind a reverse proxy or Tunnel.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can overly permissive HTTP signature parsing break behind a proxy if a middleware reads raw stream chunks incorrectly or strips body bytes?

options.text: Webhook HMAC signatures are hashed over exact raw request bytes (`await request.body()`); re-serializing JSON before checking breaks whitespace/key ordering.
options.explanation: Correct! Always verify HMAC digests against exact raw request body bytes before parsing Pydantic JSON.

options.text: Because reverse proxies turn SHA256 into MD5.
options.explanation: Proxies forward bodies intact; handlers re-serializing JSON break exact byte match.

options.text: Because HTTPS strips all HTTP bodies.
options.explanation: HTTPS encrypts transport; bodies arrive intact after TLS termination.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Verify webhook HMAC signatures against raw body bytes before JSON re-serialization.

checkpoints.title: What Cloudflare Actually Provides
checkpoints.summary: Separate Cloudflare's concrete building blocks—DNS, proxied edge WAF/TLS, Tunnel, Access, and Workers—from magic-wand misconceptions.
learningObjectives: Describe the distinct responsibility of DNS, Edge Proxy/WAF, Tunnel, Zero Trust Access, and Workers.
Know what happens to origin IP secrecy, DDoS protection, and caching when orange-cloud Proxy is enabled vs DNS-only.
Avoid misconfiguring caching on dynamic API/webhook routes.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Many learners hear 'use Cloudflare!' and think Cloudflare is one giant mysterious thing. In truth, Cloudflare is a toolbox of distinct focused products: (1) **DNS** (answers domain lookups cleanly), (2) **Proxied Edge / TLS / WAF** (hides your VPS IP, handles HTTPS certs, filters bots & rate-limits bursts), (3) **Tunnel (`cloudflared`)** (connects an internal server outbound without opening router/firewall ports), (4) **Access** (Zero Trust SSO gate in front of internal admin tools), and (5) **Workers** (runs small stateless JS/TS edge functions). Knowing *which* box solves *which* problem prevents dangerous security holes!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Important subtle operational edge case: When orange-cloud proxy sits in front of dynamic APIs/n8n UI, **never enable aggressive 'Cache Everything' rules on API or webhook endpoints**, or POST/GET dynamic responses could serve stale data or fail webhooks! Use Cloudflare WAF custom rules for rate limiting (`429` protection) and strict `Full (Strict)` SSL mode. Keep large heavy long-running downloads/SSE streams mindful of Cloudflare edge proxy HTTP idle timeouts (~100s on free/pro plans—yet another reason async `202` jobs win!).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Clear product boundaries let you leverage free/low-cost edge protection safely without shooting webhook caching or timeouts in the foot.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Whenever placing Cloudflare DNS, WAF, Tunnel, or Access in front of VPS/self-hosted automation endpoints.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't turn on HTML/API response caching on authenticated REST endpoints, n8n UI, or dynamic webhook routes!

examples.title: Cloudflare Edge Timeout & Caching Sanity Check
examples.description: Watch edge timeouts (~100s) and keep APIs dynamic (`Bypass Cache`).
examples.code:
Product           Role in AI Automation Stack
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cloudflare DNS    Resolves n8n.acme.com & api.acme.com reliably
Edge Proxy & WAF  Masks VPS IP, terminates TLS, blocks DDoS & request floods
Cloudflare Tunnel Connects local/private server outbound cleanly (NO open ports!)
Cloudflare Access Protects human admin UIs (e.g. internal dashboard) with SSO OTP
Cloudflare Worker Tiny edge script (e.g. webhook pre-filter / lightweight redirect)

GOTCHA #1: Edge HTTP read timeout (~100s) -> use async 202 jobs for long AI work!
GOTCHA #2: Never cache /webhook/* or /v1/* authenticated responses!

checkpoints.practiceTask: Map 4 needs—(a) Stop bot flood hitting `/v1/triage`, (b) Expose private homelab without port-forwarding, (c) Put Google SSO in front of internal admin dashboard, (d) Resolve domain name—to exact Cloudflare tools.
acceptanceCriteria: Maps correctly: (a) Edge WAF / Rate Limiting, (b) Tunnel, (c) Access, (d) DNS.
Notes async 202 necessity due to proxy read-timeout ceilings.
commonMistakes: Enabling 'Cache Everything' across an API/n8n domain (leaking user responses or breaking UI logins!).
Expecting synchronous 3-minute LLM runs to survive Cloudflare's ~100s edge request timeout without returning `524 Timeout`.
Assuming DNS-only (grey cloud) runs Cloudflare WAF or hides your server IP—only proxied mode routes through Edge.

quizQuestions.prompt: An n8n workflow calls `https://api.acme-ops.com/v1/heavy-research` synchronously through Cloudflare Proxy, and after ~100 seconds receives `524 A Timeout Occurred`. Why, and how do you fix it cleanly?

options.text: Cloudflare's edge proxy enforces ~100s response timeouts; switch long AI runs to `202 Accepted` async job + webhook callback.
options.explanation: Correct! Edge proxies cut off long idle synchronous HTTP responses; async job + callback handles arbitrary work safely.

options.text: Because Pydantic failed validation after 100s.
options.explanation: 524 is specifically Cloudflare waiting on an origin response too long.

options.text: Turn on Cache Everything so Cloudflare answers in 0ms.
options.explanation: Caching never solves unique dynamic POST research runs.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Design long-running AI endpoints asynchronously (`202` + callback/poll) rather than fighting edge timeouts.

quizQuestions.prompt: What happens if you accidentally leave Cloudflare DNS set to `'DNS only'` (grey cloud) instead of `'Proxied'` (orange cloud)?

options.text: Clients resolve and connect directly to your origin IP, bypassing Cloudflare's WAF, DDoS shield, and edge SSL.
options.explanation: Correct! Grey cloud is pure DNS; WAF/edge rules require orange-cloud Proxy or Tunnel.

options.text: Cloudflare automatically starts Cloudflare Access SSO.
options.explanation: Access only intercepts proxied/tunneled traffic passing through Cloudflare Edge.

options.text: Your domain disappears completely.
options.explanation: DNS still returns the record—it just routes straight to origin.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Verify proxy status (orange cloud vs grey DNS-only) when configuring edge protections.

checkpoints.title: Cloudflare DNS Versus Tunnel Versus Access Versus Workers
checkpoints.summary: Master the critical distinctions between DNS, Tunnel, Access, and Workers so you never deploy an exposed endpoint thinking a Tunnel secured it.
learningObjectives: Compare DNS, Tunnel, Access, and Workers cleanly across Purpose, Auth Enforcement, and Compute.
Combine Tunnel + Access appropriately for internal dashboards vs Service Tokens/app-level auth for machine webhooks.
Explain exactly what breaks if you swap one component thinking they're interchangeable.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Here is the exact breakdown worth memorizing: **DNS** tells browsers *where to go*. **Tunnel** builds an encrypted private bridge *back to your server* without opening router/firewall ports. **Access** checks *which human or service identity* is allowed through Cloudflare's edge (like an ID badge scanner at the front gate). **Workers** runs tiny *stateless scripts* right on Cloudflare's edge servers. Mixing them up causes real security mistakes—especially assuming a Tunnel includes Access authentication automatically (it doesn't!).
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: How they compose cleanly: (1) Internal Human Admin UI (`dash.internal.com`): DNS -> **Tunnel** -> **Access** (Email/Google/GitHub SSO policy) -> Origin Admin App. Note: **Access blocks unauthenticated SaaS webhooks** unless bypassed carefully for specific signed webhook paths or paired with Cloudflare Access Service Tokens (`CF-Access-Client-Id` / `CF-Access-Client-Secret`)! (2) Machine-to-Machine Public Webhook (`api.acme.com/webhooks/stripe`): DNS -> Tunnel/Proxy -> Origin FastAPI verifying cryptographic **HMAC signature / Bearer Token** directly in code.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Putting Access SSO in front of a third-party webhook silently breaks SaaS callbacks (redirects Stripe/Slack to a login page!), while leaving a Tunnel without Access/app auth exposes internal dashboards publicly.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Select **Access** for human logins + Zero Trust service tokens; **Tunnel** for port-less origin connectivity; **Workers** for edge routing/filtering; **DNS** always.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never drop Access SSO login redirects in front of external SaaS webhook URLs without exempting ONLY the cryptographically signed webhook path!

examples.title: Composing Tunnel + Access vs. Signed Webhook Ingress
examples.description: Human dashboards get Cloudflare Access SSO; automated webhook callbacks use signed route auth.
examples.code:
CASE A: Internal Admin / Ops Dashboard (admin.acme-ops.com)
  Browser -> DNS -> Cloudflare Edge -> [Access Policy: Allow @acme-ops.com via Google SSO]
         -> Cloudflare Tunnel -> Internal Dashboard (:3000)

CASE B: External SaaS Webhook (flow.acme-ops.com/webhook/gmail-triage)
  Gmail / SaaS -> DNS -> Cloudflare Edge (Bypass interactive login redirect!)
              -> Cloudflare Tunnel -> n8n / FastAPI (Verifies HMAC signature or Bearer Token!)
