checkpoints.practiceTask: Design the Cloudflare Access + Tunnel policy for ONE n8n domain (`flow.acme.com`) where `/webhook/*` must receive signed SaaS POSTs while everything else (`/` editor UI) demands employee SSO.
acceptanceCriteria: Protects n8n editor UI (`/`) strictly via Access SSO + n8n auth.
Exempts ONLY `/webhook/*` from interactive login redirect while enforcing cryptographic token/HMAC verification inside n8n/FastAPI.
commonMistakes: Applying a global Access login policy to `flow.acme.com/*`—breaking every external webhook because Stripe/Slack hits a Cloudflare login HTML redirect!
Thinking a Cloudflare Worker handles full Docker Python dependency graphs like FastAPI + LangGraph.
Exposing admin endpoints over Tunnel with zero Access policy and weak default passwords.

quizQuestions.prompt: You put Cloudflare Access (Google SSO login) across `n8n.acme.com/*`. Now you log into the UI safely—but Slack webhooks calling `https://n8n.acme.com/webhook/approval` suddenly fail with HTML login pages! Why?

options.text: External automated webhook servers don't have Google SSO cookies; scope Access Bypass specifically to signed `/webhook/*` paths (while verifying webhook tokens in n8n) and keep `/` under Access.
options.explanation: Correct! Interactive human SSO breaks headless webhook callers unless scoped properly and replaced with cryptographic webhook verification.

options.text: Because Slack blocks HTTPS.
options.explanation: Slack requires HTTPS; it failed on the interactive Access SSO login redirect.

options.text: Because Tunnel forbids POST requests.
options.explanation: Tunnel supports all HTTP methods cleanly.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Protect UI routes with Access SSO; protect machine `/webhook/*` routes with cryptographic tokens/HMAC or Access Service Tokens.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which Cloudflare component creates an outbound encrypted connector from inside your private server so you do NOT open firewall ports 80/443?

options.text: Cloudflare Tunnel (`cloudflared`).
options.explanation: Correct! `cloudflared` establishes outbound encrypted tunnels from origin to Cloudflare Edge.

options.text: Cloudflare DNS.
options.explanation: DNS resolves hostnames; it doesn't bridge private NATs.

options.text: Cloudflare Workers.
options.explanation: Workers executes JS/TS at the edge, not private origin tunneling alone.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Tunnel = connectivity; Access = Zero Trust identity gate; DNS = name lookup; Workers = edge compute.

checkpoints.title: Why Cloudflare Tunnel Does NOT Replace Hosting or Authentication
checkpoints.summary: Eliminate the #1 self-hosting fallacy: `cloudflared` only transports traffic—your origin still provides compute/uptime and your app must still enforce auth.
learningObjectives: Explain clearly why Tunnel != Hosting and why Tunnel != Authentication.
Verify defense-in-depth: app-level bearer/HMAC checks STILL run inside FastAPI even behind Cloudflare Access.
Identify what breaks if origin services stop, lose power, or skip internal auth verification.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Let's say this out loud because hundreds of newcomers trip over it: **Cloudflare Tunnel is a secure cable—NOT a cloud server and NOT a bouncer!** (1) **It is NOT hosting**: your actual FastAPI, Postgres, and n8n processes STILL consume real CPU/RAM/disk somewhere else (a VPS or dedicated server). If that machine crashes or shuts down, the tunnel breaks. (2) **It is NOT authentication**: once a tunnel points `api.myproject.com` to `localhost:8000`, the *entire internet* can immediately reach your API unless you ALSO add Cloudflare Access AND/OR token authentication in Python!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Architectural defense-in-depth rule: Always assume edge network layers might be bypassed or misconfigured during a rule edit. Therefore: (1) Origin FastAPI validates Bearer/HMAC credentials (or signed `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` JWT verification if trusting Access) directly in middleware/dependencies; (2) Every protected route enforces per-tenant authorization; (3) Uptime depends completely on resilient always-on host hardware + systemd/Docker restart policies (`restart: unless-stopped`), not merely the tunnel daemon.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Believing Tunnel 'magically hosts and locks down' an app causes both catastrophic uptime surprises (laptop closed!) and completely unauthenticated public API exposures.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Apply this checklist before ever trusting any tunneled URL with real credentials, webhooks, or internal company dashboards.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never skip FastAPI auth middleware simply because 'it runs behind a Cloudflare Tunnel'.

examples.title: FastAPI Origin Verification (Never Trust Unauthenticated Tunnel Traffic)
examples.description: Keep cryptographic verification inside Python even when traffic enters via reverse proxy or Tunnel.
examples.code:
import secrets
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, Header

def require_service_token(authorization: str | None = Header(default=None)) -> None:
    expected = f"Bearer {SETTINGS.internal_bearer_token.get_secret_value()}"
    if not authorization or not secrets.compare_digest(authorization, expected):
        # Tunnel connectivity does NOT substitute for verifying identity inside the app!
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Unauthorized service caller")

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write a 3-point pre-launch test verifying (1) origin process runs 24/7 on a dedicated host, (2) unauthenticated `curl` against the tunnel hostname returns `401`/`403`, and (3) valid bearer token succeeds.
acceptanceCriteria: Explicitly tests unauthenticated `curl` from an outside network (must reject with 401 or Access block!).
Verifies origin restarts cleanly on reboot (`restart: unless-stopped`).
commonMistakes: Publishing a bare Cloudflare Tunnel URL to `http://localhost:8000` with zero Access policy and zero Python auth.
Running business-critical webhooks over a tunnel from a personal laptop that sleeps every night.
Trusting `X-Forwarded-User` headers in Python without verifying the upstream token/JWT signature.

quizQuestions.prompt: You run `uvicorn` on a home server and connect a Cloudflare Tunnel pointing `triage.example.com` -> `http://127.0.0.1:8000`, with NO Access policy and NO FastAPI auth code. Who can invoke `POST https://triage.example.com/triage`?

options.text: Anyone on the public internet, draining your LLM quota immediately—because Tunnel alone provides connectivity, not authentication.
options.explanation: Correct! Pair tunnels with real authentication (Access / app-level Bearer/HMAC checks) immediately.

options.text: Only people plugged into your home Wi-Fi.
options.explanation: Cloudflare Tunnel exposes that service publicly across the internet.

options.text: Only Cloudflare employees.
options.explanation: Once routed on public DNS without Access policies, the public edge forwards all internet traffic.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Tunnel != Hosting, and Tunnel != Authentication.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why keep Python `require_service_token` verification inside FastAPI even if Cloudflare Access is ALSO configured upstream?

options.text: Defense in depth: if an Access rule is accidentally loosened or traffic enters internally, your Python service still rejects unauthenticated requests.
options.explanation: Correct! Never depend on a single upstream checkbox as your only safeguard.

options.text: Because FastAPI deletes JSON payloads without a `Header` parameter.
options.explanation: FastAPI doesn't require auth unless you code it—which is why adding it matters!

options.text: Because Cloudflare requires FastAPI tokens to route DNS.
options.explanation: App auth protects your backend independently.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Enforce authentication at your application boundary too (defense in depth).

checkpoints.title: Protecting Internal Tools and Admin Endpoints
checkpoints.summary: Lock down `/admin`, Swagger `/docs`, Prometheus metrics, n8n UI, and vector-DB dashboards so attackers can't inspect or trigger them.
learningObjectives: Disable or authenticate FastAPI `/docs`, `/redoc`, and `/openapi.json` on internet-facing APIs.
Isolate admin/ops endpoints (`/admin/reindex`, `/metrics`) onto private networks or require admin SSO/RBAC.
Verify every human approval webhook/UI confirms genuine operator identity.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Notice something sneaky about FastAPI defaults: by default, `FastAPI()` exposes interactive `/docs` and `/openapi.json` to *the whole world*—giving any scanner a tidy map of every endpoint and parameter you built! Worse, engineers often add a quick `POST /admin/reingest-docs` or `GET /metrics` route forgetting to guard it with admin authorization. Internal admin UIs, metrics, Qdrant dashboards, and n8n editors belong strictly behind VPN/Tunnel+Access SSO AND strict role checks.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Internal tooling security practices: (1) Construct production FastAPI apps with `docs_url=None, redoc_url=None, openapi_url=None` when public-facing (keep enabled in staging/internal dev); (2) Never expose database UIs (pgAdmin, Qdrant dashboard, Redis insight) directly on public DNS—access via SSH port-forward (`ssh -L`) or Zero Trust Access SSO; (3) Enforce explicit `require_admin_role` checks on administrative mutation endpoints, distinct from ordinary webhook service tokens.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Overly exposed `/docs`, metrics endpoints, and admin dashboards hand attackers reconnaissance maps and direct escalation triggers.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before putting any FastAPI, n8n, vector DB, or approval UI onto a publicly reachable server.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't break legitimate external webhook endpoints by blocking them too—separate public webhook ingress cleanly from human admin interfaces.

examples.title: Hardening Production FastAPI Docs & Admin Routes
examples.description: Hide public OpenAPI explorer in prod and separate admin role verification cleanly.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Inspect your service's route table and mark every route as: (a) Public signed webhook, (b) Service-to-service authenticated API, or (c) Admin/Dev only (must be hidden/SSO-gated).
acceptanceCriteria: Disables public Swagger/OpenAPI on external production deployments.
Applies stricter admin/SSO authorization to administrative mutation endpoints than normal caller tokens.
commonMistakes: Exposing Qdrant (`:6333`), Postgres (`:5432`), or Redis (`:6379`) UIs on public internet ports.
Protecting `/admin/delete-index` with only the regular client webhook token instead of separate admin privileges (broken AuthZ!).
Leaving `/docs` open publicly on external internet endpoints.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why might leaving Qdrant's dashboard or FastAPI's `/admin/reindex` exposed behind the exact same bearer token used by a lightweight webhook caller be dangerous?

options.text: It violates least-privilege authorization (`AuthZ`)—compromise of a normal caller token shouldn't grant destructive admin powers.
options.explanation: Correct! Separate admin privileges and lock internal UIs/routes behind Access/VPN + explicit admin roles.

options.text: Because `/admin` paths cannot accept JSON.
options.explanation: Admin routes parse JSON fine; privilege separation is the vulnerability.

options.text: Because Qdrant disables cosine distance when behind HTTPS.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Keep internal tools private (Access/SSH/VPN) and separate admin roles from regular service tokens.

quizQuestions.prompt: How should engineers securely open an internal Postgres admin tool or private Prometheus dashboard hosted on a VPS without adding a public subdomain?

options.text: Use an encrypted SSH tunnel (`ssh -L`) or Zero Trust Private Access rather than exposing database admin ports publicly.
options.explanation: Correct! SSH port forwarding and Zero Trust tunnels let operators connect securely while keeping ports completely closed publicly.

options.text: Open port 8080 publicly on the VPS and hope nobody guesses the IP.
options.explanation: Bots scan all public IPv4 ranges within minutes.

options.text: Disable UFW firewall temporarily during admin work.
options.explanation: Leaving firewalls off invites rapid intrusion.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Inspect internal tools via SSH tunnels or Zero Trust Access—never via unguarded public ports.

checkpoints.title: Health Checks and Uptime Monitoring
checkpoints.summary: Build meaningful `/health` and `/ready` probes plus external uptime checks so dead workers or expired DB pools page you before customers notice.
learningObjectives: Separate `/healthz` (process alive: returns 200 immediately) from `/readyz` (dependencies connected: verifies DB/Redis reachability).
Configure Docker Compose `healthcheck:` so dependent services start only after Postgres/APIs are truly ready.
Use external uptime pingers (checking TLS + HTTP 200 every 1–5 min) instead of relying solely on inside-host checks.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: You reboot your VPS: FastAPI starts in 0.5 seconds, returns HTTP 200 on `/health`, and *immediately starts crashing* on real requests because Postgres took 4 seconds to finish booting! Separating **liveness (`/healthz`)** ('Is the Python event loop alive?') from **readiness (`/readyz`)** ('Can FastAPI actually query Postgres right now?') prevents Docker and load balancers from sending traffic to half-booted containers. And running an external uptime monitor checks DNS + TLS + reverse proxy + origin all at once!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Liveness vs Readiness pattern: (1) `/healthz` stays trivial (`{'status': 'ok'}`)—never call paid LLM APIs inside frequent healthchecks (burns tokens AND cascades failures!); (2) `/readyz` runs lightweight non-destructive probes (`SELECT 1` on Postgres with a 2s timeout, returning `503 Service Unavailable` if unavailable); (3) Docker Compose `healthcheck` + `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` guarantees deterministic startup ordering; (4) External synthetic checks detect expired certs, DNS errors, or sleepy origin hosts even when internal containers think they're fine.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Silent half-failures—dead worker queues, crashed tunnels, expired TLS certificates—get caught within minutes instead of days.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Add `/healthz`, `/readyz`, Docker healthchecks, and an external uptime monitor on every deployed backend.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: NEVER call an external LLM API (`client.responses.create(...)`) inside `/healthz` or `/readyz`—that wastes money every 15 seconds and takes your app offline whenever OpenAI has a tiny blip!

examples.title: FastAPI Readiness Check + Docker Compose Health Ordering
examples.description: Never hit LLMs in health checks; check lightweight DB connectivity with short timeouts.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write a Compose `healthcheck:` block hitting `/readyz` every 15s and explain why calling OpenAI inside `/readyz` is a huge anti-pattern.
acceptanceCriteria: Probes only local app/DB dependencies with short timeouts; zero paid LLM calls in healthchecks.
Combines container healthcheck with external uptime monitoring.
commonMistakes: Calling an external paid LLM inside `/health` every 30 seconds (burning money & failing liveness during upstream rate limits!).
Returning `200 OK` on `/readyz` even when Postgres or queue workers are completely down.
Monitoring only from localhost on the same VPS—if the VPS loses internet or power, internal monitors never notify you!

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is calling an LLM API (`gpt-...`) inside your 30-second Docker `/health` check a terrible idea?

options.text: It burns tokens continuously and causes Docker to restart your healthy API container whenever the upstream LLM has brief rate limits or latency.
options.explanation: Correct! Health probes should stay fast, free, and check only your process and direct internal stores.

options.text: Because FastAPI forbids outbound calls inside GET routes.
options.explanation: GET routes can call outbound APIs technically—operationally it creates cost and cascading restarts.

options.text: Because LLMs always return 404 on `/health`.
options.explanation: Cost + cascading failure coupling is why you avoid LLM health checks.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Keep `/healthz` trivial and `/readyz` scoped to fast internal DB/queue connectivity—never external LLM calls.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why add an *external* uptime monitor hitting your public HTTPS endpoint even if Docker runs local healthchecks on the VPS?

options.text: External monitors verify the full chain—DNS, TLS expiry, Cloudflare Tunnel/proxy, and origin host—and alert you if the whole VPS freezes.
options.explanation: Correct! On-box checks can't fire alerts when the machine itself loses power or network.

options.text: External monitors double as database backups.
options.explanation: Backups require explicit snapshot/dump jobs.

options.text: External monitors replace HTTPS certificates automatically.
options.explanation: Monitors detect expired certs; proxies renew them.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Combine container readiness checks with external uptime pings verifying DNS, TLS, and edge routing.

checkpoints.title: Least Privilege and Key Rotation
checkpoints.summary: Scope every API token to the bare minimum permissions and environment needed, and build habits for clean zero-downtime key rotation.
learningObjectives: Apply the Principle of Least Privilege: separate read vs write keys, dev vs prod keys, and low spend caps.
Rotate leaked or aging bearer tokens and webhook secrets without downtime via dual-valid-key transition windows.
Configure provider API spend alerts and hard monthly limits so a leaked dev key cannot bankrupt you.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Suppose you accidentally leak an API key—or a teammate leaves the project. If every project shares ONE `'master_admin_api_key'` with unlimited billing across OpenAI, Gmail, Slack, and CRM, rotating that key breaks *everything simultaneously* and puts your entire billing account at risk! **Least privilege** means every service gets its own narrowly scoped key (`triage-prod-llm` with a capped monthly budget, CRM read-only token for lookups, separate staging keys). And **dual-key acceptance** lets you rotate tokens smoothly with zero downtime.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Zero-downtime rotation protocol for bearer/webhook secrets: (1) Configure FastAPI to accept `{CURRENT_SECRET, NEXT_SECRET}` temporarily during rollout; (2) Issue new secret into `NEXT_SECRET`, deploy FastAPI; (3) Update n8n HTTP Request / credential to send the new secret; (4) Verify logs show zero callers on old key, then retire old secret (`{NEXT_SECRET}` becomes `CURRENT_SECRET`). Scope all SaaS OAuth tokens minimally (read-only Gmail vs full account delete).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Blast-radius containment and painless rotation separate amateur credentials from maintainable production ops.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Every time provisioning LLM keys, CRM tokens, Slack bots, or service-to-service secrets.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't reuse production keys inside local laptops, Jupyter notebooks, or test scripts.

examples.title: Zero-Downtime Secret Rotation Support in FastAPI
examples.description: Accept active + next rotated token during rollout so n8n updates never cause 401 gaps.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write out the 4-step rotation sequence to swap the bearer token shared between n8n and FastAPI with zero dropped webhook events.
acceptanceCriteria: Enables both old and new token temporarily in FastAPI before switching n8n.
Retires the old token only after confirming n8n uses the new credential cleanly.
commonMistakes: Sharing one master API key across dev laptops, staging, and production.
Leaving LLM API keys uncapped with zero hard spend alerts.
Rotating a single secret immediately on FastAPI before updating n8n—causing outages during deploy.

quizQuestions.prompt: How do you rotate a shared webhook bearer token between n8n and FastAPI with zero downtime?

options.text: Deploy FastAPI accepting both old & new valid tokens, switch n8n credentials to the new token, verify clean calls, then remove the old token.
options.explanation: Correct! Supporting overlapping active tokens prevents 401 failures mid-cutover.

options.text: Delete the old token in FastAPI immediately and rush to edit n8n manually while webhooks fail.
options.explanation: Hard swap drops live traffic.

options.text: Store tokens publicly in Git so both pull at the same time.
options.explanation: Never store secrets in Git.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Support temporary dual-valid tokens for seamless zero-downtime key rotation.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why separate dev/test API keys from production API keys with tight provider spending limits?

options.text: To isolate blast radius if a laptop/dev environment leaks a key and enforce independent billing caps.
options.explanation: Correct! Separate keys + hard limits cap maximum financial and operational exposure.

options.text: Because FastAPI rejects development keys over HTTPS.
options.explanation: Blast-radius containment is the security/cost reason.

options.text: Because dev keys run 10x faster.
options.explanation: Isolation & spend caps are the real benefit.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Scope keys narrowly by environment and minimum permissions, with hard billing limits.

checkpoints.title: Database, Vector Store, and Workflow Backups
checkpoints.summary: Automate encrypted off-box backups AND actually test restore drills for Postgres, n8n workflow JSONs, and document corpora.
learningObjectives: Identify every stateful store needing backup: n8n workflows/credentials metadata, Postgres/LangGraph checkpoints, and source RAG documents.
Explain why copying backup files ONLY onto the same VPS disk does NOT protect against server disk loss.
Test restore drills periodically—because an untested backup is just a hopeful file.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Here is an operational truth nobody forgets once burned: **an untested backup stored on the exact same VPS disk is NOT a backup!** If that VPS filesystem corrupts or gets deleted, both your live DB and its backup disappear together! For your AI automation stack, ask: *'If my server caught fire 10 minutes from now, how do I restore (1) n8n workflows, (2) Postgres + LangGraph checkpoints, (3) source knowledge-base files to rebuild vectors cleanly, and (4) env secrets?'* Practice restoring onto a test database *before* an actual emergency.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Backup layers: (1) **Code & Workflows**: version-controlled Git repo (FastAPI, prompts, evals, exported sanitized n8n workflow JSONs); (2) **Relational & Checkpoint State**: scheduled `pg_dump` (or managed DB PITR snapshots) encrypted and shipped **off-host** (S3/R2/Backblaze B2 object storage) with retention rotation; (3) **RAG Source Documents**: back up original source files + metadata cleanly—you can always re-chunk/re-embed from raw docs! (4) Run quarterly dry-run restores into an isolated container checking row counts and n8n workflow boots.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Disks die, `DELETE` without `WHERE` happens, and upgrades fail; tested off-host backups make disasters boring 15-minute recoveries instead of company-ending losses.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before treating any automation stack as production-ready.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never skip backing up raw source documents assuming a vector index snapshot alone covers re-embedding needs—keep source docs backed up too!

examples.title: Automated Off-Host Postgres Backup + Verified Restore Check
examples.description: Always test restoring dumps into a clean scratch container—don't trust silent cron jobs.
examples.code:
# 1. Automated logical backup (run via cron/systemd timer -> upload off-host to R2/S3):
pg_dump --format=custom --no-owner "$DATABASE_URL" > "/tmp/triage_$(date +%F).dump"
# Upload encrypted artifact to off-host object storage, then clean local /tmp file!

# 2. Periodic RESTORE verification drill in a clean disposable test container:
pg_restore --clean --if-exists --dbname="$STAGING_TEST_DB_URL" "/tmp/triage_latest.dump"
psql "$STAGING_TEST_DB_URL" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM checkpoints;"

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write a 4-item Disaster Recovery Checklist covering how you recover after total VPS loss: (1) Code & n8n JSONs, (2) Postgres/Checkpoints, (3) RAG source docs, (4) Env secrets.
acceptanceCriteria: Explicitly separates off-host backup storage from primary compute VPS.
Includes a tested restore verification step (not backup creation alone).
commonMistakes: Storing cron backups inside `/root/backups/` on the exact same failing disk.
Backing up ONLY n8n workflows while forgetting the database/encryption key (`N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) needed to decrypt saved credentials!
Never testing `pg_restore` once—discovering months later dumps were 0 bytes due to bad credentials.

quizQuestions.prompt: You run nightly `pg_dump` saving `.dump` files into `/var/backups` on the same VPS running Postgres and n8n. Why is this inadequate for production disaster recovery?

options.text: If the VPS disk fails, is compromised, or is accidentally wiped, all backups on that disk are lost too—ship encrypted backups off-host and test restores.
options.explanation: Correct! True backups live off-host in separate object storage and are regularly restore-tested.

options.text: Because `pg_dump` skips tables containing integers.
options.explanation: `pg_dump` captures full schema & data; single-disk co-location is the risk.

options.text: Because Cloudflare deletes `/var/backups` automatically.
options.explanation: Host failure/disk loss is the real hazard.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Store encrypted backups off-host and prove they work through real restore drills.

quizQuestions.prompt: Wait—you restore a fresh n8n instance from backed-up database rows/workflows, yet ALL saved Gmail/Slack credentials fail to decrypt! What critical secret did your backup plan miss?

options.text: `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (stored in n8n's environment/config)—without the original encryption key, saved credentials in the DB cannot be decrypted.
options.explanation: Correct! Always document and securely vault `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` in your password/secrets manager alongside DB backups.

options.text: CORS middleware settings.
options.explanation: Unrelated to credential decryption.

options.text: Your Pydantic version.
options.explanation: Encryption key continuity is what unlocks stored n8n credentials.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Include `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and runtime secret vaults in your documented recovery runbook!

checkpoints.title: Defining Narrow High-Value Automation Problems
checkpoints.summary: Replace vague 'build an AI company assistant' dreams with crisp, bounded workflows that deliver measurable reliability and value.
learningObjectives: Narrow broad ambiguous automation requests into bounded, testable slices with clear triggers and acceptance metrics.
Spot red-flag scope creep early (open-ended 'handle all customer ops automatically').
Select a wedge problem where errors are cheap to contain via human review.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: When a founder or manager asks: *'Can we build an AI agent that handles all customer support and refunds automatically?'*, an average freelancer says *'Sure!'* and spends 3 months building a brittle mess. A senior AI Automation Engineer replies: *'Let's inspect the last 200 tickets first. Notice 45% are repetitive shipping-status + policy lookup drafts? Let's automate **triage classification + policy-grounded draft generation for human 1-click approval** first—with zero autonomous financial mutations—and measure real time saved in week one!'*
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Narrow problem scoping framework: specify (1) Exact trigger event (`new support ticket webhook`), (2) Bounded action space (`classify into 4 categories + retrieve cited KB + draft response`), (3) Explicit exclusion boundaries (`never issue refunds > $0 autonomously; escalate billing disputes immediately`), and (4) Verification baseline (`measure triage accuracy & drafting speed against manual baseline`). High-value wedges combine high repetitive volume, structured inputs, and clear review gates.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Narrow scope makes evaluation unambiguous, latency predictable, and business trust achievable in weeks instead of stalled never-finished multi-agent experiments.
checkpoints.whenToUse: At the start of every client project, internal initiative, or capstone portfolio build.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't pitch 'fully autonomous end-to-end replacement of humans' where accuracy tolerances or failure costs remain unvalidated.

examples.title: Refining Vague Pitch -> Production Wedge Scope
examples.description: Turn unmeasurable hype into a crisp shippable engineering contract.
examples.code:
VAGUE PITCH (High failure risk):
  "Build an autonomous AI agent to solve all support emails end to end."

SCOPED PRODUCTION WEDGE (High reliability & value):
  - Trigger: New ticket arrives via Gmail/Webhook in n8n.
  - Scope: Classify into [billing, bug, account, general] + retrieve cited KB articles
           + generate concise draft reply inside Pydantic schema.
  - Safety boundary: Zero auto-emails or refunds; route draft to Slack/Helpdesk
                     for 1-click human approval or edit.
  - Non-goals (v1): Multi-turn live phone chat, billing system write access.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Take a vague goal like 'Automate sales research and outreach with AI' and narrow it into a concrete v1 wedge with Explicit Trigger, Bounded Output, Exclusion Boundary, and Human Gate.
acceptanceCriteria: Defines exact trigger, structured output contract, and explicit non-goals.
Includes a clean human oversight boundary before external customer emails.
commonMistakes: Saying 'yes' to vague 'automate everything' briefs with no defined acceptance criteria.
Automating rare ultra-complex edge cases first instead of high-frequency structured wedges.
Skipping explicit 'Out of Scope for v1' lists.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does scoping v1 to 'triage + policy-grounded draft for human 1-click approval' outperform pitching 'fully autonomous customer replies + refunds'?

options.text: It delivers rapid value on high-volume work while bounding failure risk cleanly until evaluations earn deeper autonomy.
options.explanation: Correct! Narrow, observable, human-gated wedges ship fast and build real trust.

options.text: Because LLMs cannot output JSON.
options.explanation: Structured outputs work fine—failure cost and trust boundaries drive smart scoping.

options.text: Because n8n cannot call REST APIs.
options.explanation: n8n integrates cleanly with REST APIs.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Narrow scope + explicit human gates win reliability and business trust.

quizQuestions.prompt: What belongs explicitly inside your 'Non-Goals / Out of Scope for v1' list?

options.text: High-risk autonomous actions and obscure 1% edge channels intentionally deferred so v1 stays rock-solid.
options.explanation: Correct! Clear non-goals protect schedules and prevent hidden regressions.

options.text: Unit tests and error handling.
options.explanation: Testing and safety belong in v1 from day one!

options.text: Pydantic validation.
options.explanation: Data contracts are non-negotiable baseline hygiene.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Document explicit v1 non-goals before writing architecture code.

checkpoints.title: Requirements and Scoping
checkpoints.summary: Write crisp engineering specs covering functional contracts, latency/throughput limits, failure behavior, and non-functional constraints.
learningObjectives: Document inputs, outputs, error contracts, expected peak request rate, and timeout budgets before coding.
Define fallback behavior when external LLM providers or third-party APIs experience downtime.
Confirm compliance constraints (data residency, zero training on customer data, retention limits).
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Half of automation bugs aren't coding bugs—they're missing requirements! *'Wait, can emails arrive with 10 MB PDF attachments?' 'What happens when OpenAI returns 503 during peak Monday morning—do tickets get lost or queued cleanly?'* Writing a tight 1-page engineering requirements spec upfront surfaces payload caps, concurrency limits, fallback behavior, and privacy constraints before you hardcode assumptions.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Production requirements spec checklist: (1) **API & Payload Contracts** (max email size, allowed attachments, required metadata, Pydantic schemas); (2) **Volume & Concurrency** (avg vs burst tickets/min, batch sizes); (3) **Degraded-Mode Fallback** (if LLM/RAG fails after retries -> return `202` queued or route unclassified ticket cleanly to `general_human_queue` instead of dropping emails!); (4) **Compliance & Retention** (PII masking, API zero-data-retention tier).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Designing degraded fallback paths upfront keeps business operations running smoothly even when downstream AI providers wobble.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Prior to building any multi-week automation service or signing client milestones.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't turn a 1-page engineering spec into a 60-page unread bureaucracy doc; keep it tight, concrete, and test-oriented.

examples.title: 1-Page Engineering Requirements Template
examples.description: Covers contracts, traffic estimates, fallback path, and safety boundaries clearly.
examples.code:
# Spec: Support Triage Service v1
- **Expected Volume**: ~500 emails/day, bursts up to ~20/min (must not drop requests!)
- **Input Limits**: Body <= 32 KB text (truncate safely with flag); skip raw binary attachments in v1.
- **Latency Target**: Intake webhook ack < 1s (`202`); async draft posted < 15s p95.
- **Degraded Fallback**: If LLM API errors 3x -> mark `status=fallback_human`, notify ops queue; NEVER drop ticket.
- **Data Privacy**: Redact PII before logs; provider API configured with zero-data-retention.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Draft the 5-bullet spec block above for a 'Document Processing Pipeline' reading uploaded invoices into a finance queue.
acceptanceCriteria: Specifies explicit max input size / page cap and throughput assumption.
Defines exact degraded-mode behavior when extraction fails validation repeatedly.
commonMistakes: Assuming happy-path single inputs ('maybe 1 email/hour') without planning burst queues or fallback routing.
Ignoring huge email attachments or embedded base64 images blowing out FastAPI memory/context limits.
Leaving client privacy/retention assumptions unspoken until after launch.

quizQuestions.prompt: In a production support automation spec, what MUST happen if the LLM provider returns `503 Unavailable` past all retry attempts?

options.text: Route the ticket explicitly to a safe deterministic human queue (`fallback_human`) with an ops alert—never silently drop the customer's email.
options.explanation: Correct! Fail-safe fallback paths protect customers during AI outages.

options.text: Return `200 OK` and silently discard the payload.
options.explanation: Silent data loss destroys operational trust.

options.text: Fabricate a canned refund confirmation.
options.explanation: Never fake actions on failures.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Always design explicit degraded fallback paths for AI provider outages.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why define explicit max body/payload caps (e.g. `max_chars = 32_000`) inside requirements & schemas?

options.text: Unbounded forwarded email threads can blow past model context limits, exhaust RAM, and spike single-request token costs.
options.explanation: Correct! Bounding payloads enforces reliability and predictable cost.

options.text: Because Pydantic ignores fields longer than 100 chars automatically.
options.explanation: Pydantic enforces bounds only when you specify constraints!

options.text: Because JSON only allows 10 KB total.
options.explanation: JSON permits larger payloads; service bounds keep systems resilient.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Specify payload bounds and truncation/rejection rules upfront.

checkpoints.title: Service-Level Objectives
checkpoints.summary: Set realistic latency, availability, and extraction-quality SLOs grounded in measurements rather than unattainable 100% promises.
learningObjectives: Distinguish SLIs (what you measure), SLOs (internal engineering targets), and SLAs (contractual guarantees).
Define measurable reliability and quality SLOs suitable for probabilistic AI automations.
Recognize why aiming for 100.00% uptime or 100% AI accuracy guarantees burnout and false promises.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Notice nobody should promise '100% accuracy and 100% uptime forever'—even Google Search doesn't promise 100%! Instead, engineers define **SLIs** (the exact numbers measured, e.g. `p95 processing latency`, `% valid JSON outputs`, `successful ticket routing rate`) and **SLOs** (the realistic target we maintain, e.g. `99.5% of tickets routed cleanly without dropping`). When our actual error budget starts burning too fast, we freeze shiny new features and focus on stability!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Concrete AI Automation SLIs/SLOs: (1) **Intake Durability** (`99.9%` of accepted webhooks persist to DB/queue without drop); (2) **Processing Latency** (`p95 <= 12s` end-to-end async triage); (3) **Contract Reliability** (`>= 99%` structured schema pass rate after repair/retry); (4) **Quality Baseline** (regression eval pass rate `>= baseline_threshold` before deploys). Never commit externally to strict financial SLAs without backing infrastructure redundancy and upstream vendor coverage.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Concrete SLOs align engineering priorities, cost investments, and stakeholder expectations objectively.
checkpoints.whenToUse: When operating recurring business workflows or explaining system reliability targets in interviews/proposals.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never write fake pre-filled numbers claiming '99.99% uptime achieved' before measuring actual historical uptime data.

examples.title: Defining Honest SLIs vs. Realistic SLO Targets
examples.description: Keep targets concrete, measurable via logs, and distinct from fake marketing percentages.
examples.code:
Metric Domain       SLI (Measured Signal)                 SLO Target Example
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Webhook Intake      % requests saved cleanly to queue     >= 99.9% over 30 days
Async Completion    p95 seconds webhook -> Slack card     <= 15s (non-queued bursts)
Schema Integrity    % LLM calls yielding valid Pydantic   >= 99.0% (incl. 1 retry)
Eval Safety Gate    Adversarial prompt-injection suite    100% policy guard pass

checkpoints.practiceTask: Write 3 SLIs (exact metric formula) and pragmatic initial SLOs for a Document Processing Pipeline.
acceptanceCriteria: Defines exact numerator/denominator SLIs measurable from structured logs.
Separates intake durability (never lose incoming docs) from probabilistic extraction thresholds.
commonMistakes: Promising '100% AI extraction accuracy' on messy handwritten invoices.
Setting 200ms latency SLOs while calling a remote 4-second LLM API synchronously.
Reporting fake unmeasured SLO compliance numbers on a resume or portfolio page.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is separating an **Intake Durability SLO** (never drop incoming tickets) from an **AI Drafting Latency/Quality SLO** vital for automation reliability?

options.text: Even if an LLM call slows down or enters retry/fallback, queueing guarantees zero incoming customer tickets vanish silently.
options.explanation: Correct! Persistence first guarantees durability even when upstream AI lags.

options.text: Because queues run only in JavaScript.
options.explanation: Queues work across Python/Redis/Postgres cleanly.

options.text: Because intake skips authentication.
options.explanation: Intake still verifies signatures/tokens before queueing.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Separate durable intake guarantees from slower downstream AI processing targets.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the proper engineering response when weekly telemetry reveals your error budget is burning through twice your SLO target?

options.text: Pause non-urgent feature tweaks and invest cycles directly into reliability, retries, or retrieval bug fixes.
options.explanation: Correct! Error budgets turn reliability vs feature velocity into a clear engineering lever.

options.text: Delete structured logging so nobody sees the burn rate.
options.explanation: Observability must guide fixes, not hide faults.

options.text: Lower the monitoring check frequency to once a month.
options.explanation: Monitoring must stay continuous.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Use SLO error budgets to trigger stability fixes proactively.

checkpoints.title: Cost Budgeting and Rate Caps
checkpoints.summary: Protect businesses from runaway loops, bot floods, and surprise monthly invoices using multi-layer rate limits, token caps, and budget alarms.
learningObjectives: Estimate expected monthly variable LLM cost cleanly from measured tokens-per-run * daily volume.
Enforce protective caps at 3 layers: edge/API rate limit, per-workflow loop/token budget, and LLM provider billing ceiling.
Explain why runaway retries or infinite agent loops can spike 100x spend overnight without caps.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Think of deploying an AI agent with zero caps like leaving a blank corporate credit card wired to a `while True:` loop! If a buggy webhook keeps re-triggering on its own reply (a classic email-reply loop!), an uncapped automation can send 20,000 API calls before morning. **Defense in depth for cost** means placing caps at three separate doors: (1) Edge/FastAPI rate limiting (`X requests/min per caller`), (2) Graph/app loop & `max_tokens` caps, and (3) Hard monthly spend alerts + limits inside your LLM provider dashboard.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Cost containment stack: (a) Explicit `max_tokens` / `max_output_tokens` + trimmed `max_context_chars` on every model invocation; (b) `recursion_limit` + `tool_budget` in LangGraph + cycle detection preventing self-reply email loops (`if sender == our_support_email: drop!`); (c) HTTP rate limiting (Cloudflare WAF + slowapi/Redis token bucket) returning `429`; (d) Provider billing hard cap + 50%/80%/100% alerts.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Predictable bounded costs protect both solo builders and enterprise clients from sudden unexpected bills.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before putting ANY automated trigger (especially inbox listeners or public endpoints) live in production.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never skip loop-prevention checks (`ignore self-sent email / automated bounce headers`) when automating inbound email!

examples.title: Multi-Layer Cost & Loop Prevention Checklist
examples.description: Guard every cost amplification path before turning triggers ON.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Calculate a hypothetical monthly token cost formula given: `volume/day`, `avg_input_tokens`, `avg_output_tokens`, and `model_rates`, then list 3 hard safeguards preventing 10x cost explosions.
acceptanceCriteria: Identifies self-reply / vacation-responder loop detection.
Combines edge rate caps (`429`), workflow `max_steps`/`max_tokens`, and billing hard caps.
commonMistakes: Forgetting `sender != support_email` and creating an automated support-bot <-> out-of-office email ping-pong storm!
Relying only on verbal reminders without setting hard spend limits inside provider billing consoles.
Enabling infinite webhook retries in n8n on bad `4xx` prompts.

quizQuestions.prompt: An engineer automates a support inbox without checking `sender == our_support_email` or `Auto-Submitted` headers. An auto-responder replies back and forth overnight. Which 3 safeguards stop or cap this disaster?

options.text: Self-sender/auto-reply skip filters, API rate/dedup checks per thread, and hard provider billing caps + alerts.
options.explanation: Correct! Combine loop filters, deduplication/rate caps, and billing ceilings.

options.text: Setting LLM temperature to 0.
options.explanation: Temperature 0 doesn't stop webhook loops.

options.text: Adding CORS headers.
options.explanation: CORS applies only in browsers.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Prevent trigger loops explicitly and cap costs across Edge, App/Graph, and Provider billing.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why set explicit `max_output_tokens` on structured classification API calls?

options.text: Caps runaway verbose generations and bounds worst-case output latency & token cost per request.
options.explanation: Correct! Setting crisp output ceilings keeps latency and cost bounded.

options.text: Because larger `max_output_tokens` doubles DNS speed.
options.explanation: Unrelated to DNS.

options.text: To skip Pydantic validation.
options.explanation: Always keep validation enabled.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Bound input context length, output tokens, and graph iterations per call.

checkpoints.title: Data Retention and Privacy
checkpoints.summary: Establish clear data-lifecycle rules—who owns payloads, how long traces/checkpoints persist, provider training opt-outs, and right-to-delete workflows.
learningObjectives: Audit every location a user email or uploaded PDF touches (n8n execution logs, FastAPI logs, LLM vendor, DB/vector index).
Configure explicit retention TTLs (`30 days` execution logs, minimal DB fields, disabled vendor training).
Ensure document deletion (`m09_c14`) and user deletion requests remove PII across vector chunks and checkpoints cleanly.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: When you plug an email trigger into n8n, FastAPI, Postgres, Qdrant, and an OpenAI/Anthropic API, customer data now sits in **five different places** unless you actively manage retention! Good engineers map that full data trail before launch: *'How long does n8n keep raw execution payloads? Did we turn off model-provider training retention? When a customer asks to delete their account or doc, does our deletion script clean Postgres AND vector embeddings?*' Privacy compliance is way simpler when engineered upfront rather than bolted onto 6 messy stores later.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Production data-governance checklist: (1) **Minimize stored fields**: configure n8n `EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true` and `EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE` so millions of historical emails don't pile up unencrypted; (2) **Third-party LLM API settings**: verify API terms (zero-data-retention / no model training on API traffic—never feed sensitive company docs into free consumer chat UIs!); (3) **Cascading Delete**: link `doc_id`/`tenant_id` cleanly across SQL rows and vector indexes so deletion scrubs all derived chunks.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Businesses rightly reject AI tools that leak client records into vendor training pools or hoard indefinite unpruned execution logs.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before deploying workflows ingesting customer emails, HR records, invoices, or internal company docs.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never paste client secrets or unapproved confidential data into personal consumer AI accounts without explicit organizational approval.

examples.title: Audit Map: Every Place Customer Data Touches + TTL Control
examples.description: Document exact persistence window and deletion hook per subsystem.
examples.code:
System Component        What It Stores                 Retention / Privacy Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
n8n Execution History   Full input/output item JSONs   EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true (e.g. 7-14d)
FastAPI Stdout Logs     Step events + redacted IDs     PII scrubbed at logger; 30d log rotation
Postgres Checkpoints    Graph thread state             TTL cleanup job after ticket closed + N days
Vector Store (RAG)      Chunked doc text + metadata    Delete-by-doc_id / tenant_id cascade

checkpoints.practiceTask: Draw the 5-row Data Audit table above for your Document Processing capstone, specifying exactly how old invoice records get purged cleanly.
acceptanceCriteria: Accounts for n8n execution logs, app logs, DB/vector chunks, and LLM vendor retention.
Includes concrete pruning config and cascade deletion by document/tenant ID.
commonMistakes: Leaving default infinite n8n execution history storage accumulating unencrypted customer payloads for years (also crashes disk space!).
Deleting a document from Postgres while orphaned vector chunks keep getting retrieved in RAG answers.
Testing sensitive client emails inside consumer web chat interfaces where training defaults may differ from API terms.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is enabling execution log pruning (`EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE` / max age) critical on self-hosted n8n handling customer webhooks?

options.text: Default unpruned n8n history stores full raw webhook JSONs indefinitely—creating privacy liability and eventually filling your VPS disk.
options.explanation: Correct! Automatic pruning protects both privacy boundaries and database storage limits.

options.text: Because pruning turns n8n into FastAPI.
options.explanation: Pruning cleans historical execution records only.

options.text: Because pruning bypasses TLS.
options.explanation: Unrelated to TLS.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Map every store touching user data and set explicit retention TTLs + deletion cascades.

quizQuestions.prompt: A client requests immediate removal of Document `doc_882`. Which step guarantees complete removal in a RAG pipeline?

options.text: Delete both the metadata record in SQL AND all chunks carrying `doc_id='doc_882'` inside the vector/BM25 index.
options.explanation: Correct! Deleting only source PDFs leaves stale vectors surfacing leaked snippets in RAG answers.

options.text: Restart FastAPI without touching the vector store.
options.explanation: Vector databases persist across restarts.

options.text: Clear browser cache.
options.explanation: Browser cache doesn't clean server indexes.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Ensure delete pipelines remove both source files and derived vector/search chunks.

checkpoints.title: Alerting and Incident Response
checkpoints.summary: Alert on actionable failures—never noisy spam—and follow clear triage runbooks when production breaks.
learningObjectives: Design actionable alerts (uptime down, elevated 5xx spike, dead-letter queue growing, budget cap reached) vs noisy alert fatigue.
Follow a calm 4-step incident runbook: Contain/Fallback -> Gather Trace IDs -> Mitigate/Rollback -> Postmortem + Regression Test.
Avoid sending raw alerts for every single flaky transient retry that succeeded automatically on retry #2.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: If Slack pings `#alerts` 90 times a day for tiny single-retry network hiccups that recovered fine in 400ms, within three days **everyone mutes `#alerts`**—and misses the real outage! Good alerting obeys one golden rule: **only wake a human when human action or awareness is genuinely required**. When an alert fires, pair it with a tiny runbook link: *What broke? What fallback is keeping tickets safe? Which `trace_id`/log command finds the root cause in 60 seconds?*
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Alerting tiers: **Page / Immediate Alert** (uptime monitor fails 2x consecutively; error rate > 5% over 5 min; DLQ count > threshold; daily cost > 80% ceiling). **Daily Digest / Dashboard** (single transient 429 resolved by retry, normal review queue counts). Incident flow: (1) **Verify containment** (are incoming emails safely queued or routed to human fallback?); (2) **Isolate scope** (`git log` / recent prompt/config deploy? upstream OpenAI status? expired secret?); (3) **Mitigate/Rollback**; (4) **Blameless postmortem + permanent regression test**.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Calm, structured incident response turns stressful outages into predictable recoveries without dropping customer trust.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Whenever setting up Slack/email alerts or handover docs for live systems.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't alert directly on expected user validation mistakes (like `422` missing email body) unless spikes indicate a broken caller!

examples.title: Concise Incident Response Runbook Snippet
examples.description: Keep runbooks scannable under stress with immediate commands and rollback paths.
examples.code:
# Runbook: Alert `triage-5xx-spike`
1. **Check Blast Radius**: Verify n8n error branch is routing fallback tickets cleanly to `#support-manual-triage` (zero dropped tickets!).
2. **Inspect Last 50 Errors**: `docker compose logs fastapi-triage --tail=50 | jq 'select(.level=="ERROR")'`
3. **Common Causes**:
   - Expired LLM/CRM key -> verify `401` in logs -> rotate env secret.
   - Upstream LLM 503 outage -> leave safe fallback active until status recovers.
   - Broken prompt/code deploy -> rollback container image / `PROMPT_VERSION` immediately!
4. **After Recovery**: Add sanitized failing payload to `evals/regressions.json` before re-deploying.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Separate 4 events into 'Immediate Alert' vs 'Aggregate Daily Summary Only': (a) Uptime `/readyz` returns 503 for 2 mins, (b) 1 single retry on transient OpenAI 429 succeeded in 1.2s, (c) Hourly spend hits 90% budget cap, (d) Dead-letter failure queue grows by 15 stuck emails.
acceptanceCriteria: Places (a), (c), (d) in Immediate Alert and (b) in Daily Metrics/Summary.
Explains how alert fatigue compromises real incident detection.
commonMistakes: Alerting Slack on every single transient exception caught and fixed by automatic backoff retries.
Debugging blindly in panic during an outage without first verifying fallback containment.
Fixing an outage manually without adding a regression test afterward.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is firing a Slack `#alerts` notification every time a single HTTP retry recovers from a transient 429 rate limit harmful?

options.text: It creates severe alert fatigue so operators start ignoring `#alerts` and miss genuine critical outages.
options.explanation: Correct! Reserve live alerts for failures requiring awareness/action (unrecovered DLQ items, readiness outage, budget cap).

options.text: Because Slack limits webhooks to 1 message per week.
options.explanation: Human cognitive fatigue—not Slack limits—is the danger.

checkpoints.title: Rollback Planning
checkpoints.summary: Switch back cleanly to known-good container images, prompt versions, n8n workflows, or model configs within minutes when an update misbehaves.
learningObjectives: Keep immutable versioned artifacts (Docker image tags, Git tags, versioned `prompts/triage_v2.txt`, n8n workflow history) ready to revert.
Decouple risky prompt/model edits via versioned config flags where possible for rapid rollback.
Verify forward-and-backward DB schema compatibility so rolling back app code doesn't crash against newer DB tables.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Suppose you deploy `Prompt v3` + a new model name at 10:00 AM, and by 10:15 AM structured schema failures jump from 0.2% to 12%! If you pushed directly over a single mutable `:latest` Docker image or edited a single live production prompt in a UI text box with no history, you're stuck scrambling while customers suffer! **Rollback engineering** means every deploy moves forward along labeled rails (`v1.4.2`, `PROMPT_VERSION=v2`)—so reverting takes 30 seconds by flipping back to the previous verified artifact.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Rollback readiness practices: (1) Tag images immutably (`triage-api:git-a1b2c3d`, never overwrite `:latest` only!); (2) Version prompt templates and model settings explicitly in Git/config (`PROMPT_VERSION=v2`); (3) Use n8n workflow version history or Git-backed workflow JSON exports so broken workflow edits revert cleanly; (4) Perform additive database migrations (add nullable column first before deleting old columns) so rolling back Python code doesn't break existing SQL queries.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Fast safe rollbacks slash outage duration from panicked hours to boring two-minute switches.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before deploying prompt changes, model swaps, n8n routing updates, or database migrations.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never deploy destructive `DROP COLUMN` SQL migrations in the exact same release as new code before verifying the new release is stable!

examples.title: Immutable Versioned Rollback Configuration
examples.description: Deploy tagged builds and versioned prompts so reversing bad updates is a 1-line switch.

services:
  fastapi-triage:
    image: ghcr.io/acme/support-triage:v1.4.2   # Pin exact tested tag!
    environment:
      PROMPT_VERSION: "triage_v2"
      MODEL_NAME: "gpt-4o-mini"

# Bad deploy on v1.5.0 / triage_v3?
# Revert image tag back to `v1.4.2` + `triage_v2` and run `docker compose up -d`!

Editing live production prompts directly inside an unversioned admin web UI textbox.

options.text: Because `:git-sha` encrypts traffic.

checkpoints.title: Maintenance Ownership
checkpoints.summary: Assign explicit human owners, dependency update cadences, and clean handover documentation so automations don't become abandoned black boxes.
learningObjectives: Define clear post-launch ownership: who watches alerts, updates keys/dependencies, and tunes eval sets.
Prevent 'ghost automations' where the original builder moves on and nobody knows where credentials or prompts live.
Prepare a concise handover package for clients or teammates.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Notice what happens at real companies: an enthusiastic builder connects 14 n8n workflows and a custom Python API, celebrates launch, and leaves 4 months later. Nobody knows which account owns the OpenAI key, where `.env` lives, how to update the RAG knowledge base, or who receives failure alerts. Within six months, an expired SaaS OAuth token silently kills the whole workflow! **Engineering means owning the lifecycle**—assigning a clear owner, rotation calendar, and clean handover folder from day one.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Ownership & Handover Pack: (1) Named System Owner + Escalation Contact; (2) Credential & Subscription Inventory (which company-owned vault/admin email holds domains, Cloudflare, GitHub, LLM billing—NEVER personal employee emails!); (3) Routine Maintenance Cadence (monthly security/dependency check, quarterly backup restore drill, prompt/eval check when product policies change); (4) Self-service ops guide (adding/deleting KB docs safely without dev help).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Great engineers build systems that businesses can actually run safely long after initial launch—not brittle hero-only dependencies.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before completing any freelance delivery, team transition, or production launch.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never register production Cloudflare, GitHub, or billing API keys strictly under your personal developer email when delivering to an organization!

checkpoints.title: Documentation and Architecture Diagrams
checkpoints.summary: Write concise, truthful READMEs, Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), and clear ASCII/Mermaid diagrams that teammates actually read.
learningObjectives: Create a scannable project README containing architecture overview, setup steps, env vars, test commands, and security model.
Draw accurate end-to-end diagrams showing n8n triggers, FastAPI boundaries, RAG/LangGraph stores, and human gates.
Write brief Architecture Decision Records explaining *why* tools were chosen or intentionally skipped.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Imagine opening a GitHub repository where the README only says `# my-ai-agent` + three screenshots! Zero clue how to run it locally, which env vars it needs, or why LangGraph was used! Great engineering documentation respects the reader's time: (1) a clear **data-flow diagram**, (2) **exact copy-paste local run & test commands**, (3) a crisp **Why this stack / Why NOT X** summary, and (4) explicit documentation of **limitations & failure modes**.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Core documentation trio: (1) **`README.md`** (Problem -> Data-Flow Diagram -> Quickstart -> `.env` table -> `pytest` / eval commands -> Deployment & Security summary -> Limitations); (2) **Architecture Diagram** (ASCII/Mermaid illustrating HTTP/network trust boundaries, private vs public paths, and human-in-the-loop interrupts); (3) **Short ADRs** ('ADR-01: Used single FastAPI + Pydantic triage instead of autonomous multi-agent team because deterministic routing covered 100% of paths cleanly').
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Clear architecture docs and ADRs impress hiring engineers far more than flashy demo GIFs—they prove you understand trade-offs.
checkpoints.whenToUse: On every capstone project, production repository, and open-source automation blueprint.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't document untested commands or wishful planned features as if they already work—mark verified vs planned honestly!

checkpoints.title: Measuring Baseline Versus Post-Automation Outcomes
checkpoints.summary: Quantify genuine business impact by logging real baseline handling times and error rates BEFORE automating—and tracking real post-launch results.
learningObjectives: Capture concrete pre-automation baseline measurements (minutes/ticket, manual steps, error rate) before launch.
Compute honest net impact accounting for human review time, exception handling, and token/hosting costs.
Distinguish measured project outcomes from invented hype marketing claims.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: How do real engineers answer *'Was this automation actually worth building?'* You don't guess *'Saved 80% time!'*—you record an honest **before-and-after comparison**! Before writing code, sample 30 real tickets: *average triage + policy lookup + reply time = 6.5 minutes per ticket*. After deploying your human-approved draft pipeline, measure *actual human review + edit time* (say, 1.8 minutes) plus *API/hosting cost* and *override rate*. Now your ROI statement is real, transparent, and respected by technical & business leaders alike.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Net ROI equation: `Net_Benefit = (Baseline_Minutes - Review_Plus_Exception_Minutes) * Volume * Hourly_Rate - (Token_Cost + Hosting_Cost + Maintenance_Cost)`. Always include **rejection/edit rate** (`% of AI drafts requiring heavy rewrite`) and **eval pass rate on N held-out test cases** so stakeholders see realistic nuance rather than cherry-picked best-case stories.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Businesses invest repeatedly in engineers who prove real measured value honestly instead of throwing fake '10x AI' slogans.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Before pitching ROI internally or writing quantitative sections of project case studies.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: NEVER invent fake '99.4% accuracy' or '$50k saved/month' percentages when showing learning or sample portfolio builds—leave measured fields blank until YOU run and measure your own dataset!

examples.title: Honest Measured Baseline vs. Post-Launch Ledger
examples.description: Template requiring genuine measured observations—never pre-filled vanity numbers.

# Impact Ledger (Fill ONLY With Your Measured Observations)

- **Pre-Automation Baseline Handling Time**: ___ min/ticket (measured over ___ samples)
- **Post-Automation Human Review + Edit Time**: ___ min/ticket (observed)
- **Draft Approval Rate Without Major Rewrite**: ___ / ___ (%)
- **Eval Pass Rate on Held-Out Test Set**: ___ / ___ (%)
- **Measured Run Latency (p95) & Cost per Ticket**: ___ s, $___ / ticket

acceptanceCriteria: Explains why honest sample size (`35/40`) plus observed failure modes builds genuine engineering credibility.
Accounts for human review and exception-handling overhead in ROI.
commonMistakes: Fabricating unmeasured percentage gains on resumes or project cards.
Ignoring the time humans spend reviewing, correcting, and maintaining the automation when calculating net savings.
Measuring ONLY happy-path demos instead of tracking edit/rejection rates.

options.explanation: Correct! Precision, honesty about sample scope, and clear failure analysis scream senior engineer.

options.text: Write `'Deployed to Fortune 500 enterprise saving $120k/year'` to stand out.
options.explanation: Fabricated production claims fail technical interviews immediately.

options.text: Claim `'100% zero hallucination guarantee'`.
options.explanation: Probabilistic models never come with 100% hallucination immunity.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Measure real tests/baselines honestly and state exact test scope without hype.

checkpoints.title: Presenting Projects Honestly
checkpoints.summary: Turn your capstone builds into clear, humble, technically deep case studies that emphasize architecture, evaluation, security, and lessons learned.
learningObjectives: Structure portfolio case studies around Problem -> Architecture -> Validation/Guardrails -> Measured Evals -> Known Limitations.
Walk hiring engineers straight to inspectable code: Pydantic contracts, pytest evals, LangGraph interrupt, Docker/Compose setup.
Discuss real bugs you hit and fixed during testing rather than pretending everything worked smoothly first try.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Hiring managers see hundreds of shallow Twitter demos: shiny UI screenshots hiding un-validated `chat.completions` calls with zero tests! What makes a portfolio case study unforgettable in under 90 seconds? Show: (1) **Clean problem & system boundary** (why n8n handles triggers while FastAPI handles Pydantic contracts & RAG); (2) **Exact guardrails** (how you prevented prompt injection, double webhooks, and tenant leakage); (3) **Real reproducible test & eval suite** (`pytest` command + real measured score on N cases); (4) **Honest limitations & next steps**.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Case-study blueprint: open with a crisp 2-sentence summary + clean system diagram -> link directly to `schemas.py` (Pydantic contracts), `graph.py` (interrupt/state persistence), and `tests/evals/` (adversarial + golden suite) -> share genuine engineering postmortem insights ('Initially our n8n container returned ECONNREFUSED hitting localhost:8000; resolved via Compose service DNS + idempotency middleware'). Never inflate simulated benchmarks into production traffic claims.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Transparency, clean test harnesses, and real bug postmortems establish instant technical trust with senior interviewers and clients.
checkpoints.whenToUse: When polishing your GitHub project repositories, portfolio cards, or video walkthroughs.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never hide broken areas or claim untested mobile/enterprise capabilities as verified.

checkpoints.title: Interview Readiness and System Design Trade-Offs
checkpoints.summary: Articulate crisp system-design decisions under questioning: n8n vs Python, direct API vs LangChain vs LangGraph, RAG vs fine-tuning, and security.
learningObjectives: Defend architectural choices cleanly: when plain Python beats frameworks, when LangGraph wins, and when RAG beats fine-tuning.
Debug live whiteboarding/networking prompts confidently (Docker `localhost`, HTTP 401 vs 403, CORS security myth, Cloudflare Tunnel vs Access).
Walk interviewers through reliability layers: idempotency, retries, prompt-injection defense, evaluation metrics, and rollback.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: In an AI Automation Engineer interview, nobody tests whether you memorized obscure library flags—they test **how you reason through real systems and failure modes!** Notice you now command every core architectural conversation: *'Why put n8n at the trigger edge and FastAPI behind it?' 'What happens if the customer prompt asks to issue a $500 refund?' 'Why couldn't n8n reach localhost:8000 inside Docker?' 'Why won't CORS stop curl attacks?' 'How do you prove Prompt v2 actually improved without breaking urgent tickets?'* Keep answers structured: **Requirements -> Core Architecture -> Guardrails/Failure Modes -> Evals -> Trade-offs**.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Structured 5-minute system design framework: (1) **Clarify bounds** (throughput, latency sync vs async `202`, human approval need, risk level); (2) **Draw clean boundaries** (SaaS triggers -> authenticated proxy/network -> FastAPI + Pydantic -> deterministic checks -> RAG with ACLs / LangGraph checkpoint/interrupt); (3) **Pre-empt classic failure modes** (idempotency keys, exponential backoff on 429/503, raw-body HMAC verification, indirect prompt-injection defense); (4) **Verify & monitor** (component metrics Recall@K vs F1, trace IDs, PII redaction, cost caps, rollback tags).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Connecting the whole stack cleanly from TCP/HTTP sockets up through LangGraph interrupts and production operations makes you genuinely hireable as an engineer—not just a node-clicker.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Preparing for senior AI Automation Engineer interviews, client architecture discovery calls, and final portfolio reviews.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't recite buzzwords ('I'll build a multi-agent swarm on Kubernetes') without justifying why simpler deterministic steps wouldn't be safer, faster, and cheaper!

options.text: Validate inputs with Pydantic, apply deterministic amount/vendor rules in code, extract fields via bounded LLM calls, require idempotency + human interrupt approval before payouts, and evaluate with golden + adversarial pytest cases.
options.explanation: Correct! Combines contracts, deterministic policy gates, scoped AI, idempotent human oversight, and measurable evaluation.

options.text: Give a single autonomous LLM full database write access and SQL permissions so it moves fast.
options.explanation: Giving unvalidated LLMs direct financial mutation authority invites catastrophic fraud and errors.

options.text: Enable `CORS: *` so browsers trust the FastAPI port.
options.explanation: Completely misses architecture, auth, idempotency, and guardrails.

quizQuestions.prompt: An interviewer asks: 'How do you know your RAG assistant won't leak Tenant A's private HR PDF to Tenant B?' What is the single non-negotiable invariant?

options.text: Enforce server-verified caller authentication (`AuthN`) and apply mandatory tenant metadata ACL filtering (`AuthZ`) inside the retriever query BEFORE any chunks reach LLM context.
options.explanation: Correct! Filter strictly by verified tenant identity at retrieval query time—never prompt the LLM to hide leaked chunks.

options.text: Tell the LLM in the system prompt: 'Never mention other companies'.
options.explanation: Prompt-only instructions crumble under indirect prompt injection; enforce ACLs in deterministic retrieval queries.

options.text: Use fine-tuning instead so everyone shares weights.
options.explanation: Fine-tuning cannot enforce per-tenant row access controls.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Enforce tenant isolation deterministically in retrieval metadata queries before context assembly.
